label: Abijam
overview: Abijam is an alternate spelling for Abijah, used primarily in the Book of Kings to refer to the son of Rehoboam who reigned over Judah. This name variation refers to the same individual who engaged in a fierce war with Jeroboam I of Israel. Abijam's three-year reign was a time of tension and transition in the southern kingdom. While he is noted for his lack of total devotion to God, he was still used by the Lord to preserve the Davidic line in Jerusalem. His reign serves as a bridge between the fractured leadership of Rehoboam and the religious reforms of his son, Asa.

label: Abram
overview: Abram is the original name of the man who would eventually become Abraham, the great patriarch of Israel. During this phase of his life, he was a wealthy nomad living in Haran who received a radical call from God to leave everything behind and journey to an undisclosed land. The name Abram, meaning 'exalted father,' was ironic for much of his life as he and his wife Sarai remained childless. His years as Abram were characterized by a mix of profound faith, such as his departure from his homeland, and moments of fear, such as his deception in Egypt. His transformation from Abram to Abraham represents a shift from a personal identity to a national and spiritual one.

card.note: The Bible doesn't say whether he is the Alexander in the Ephesian crowd or the Alexander disciplined with Hymenaeus.

label: Amasa
overview: Commanded Absalom's army during the rebellion against David. David later promised him Joab's command. After Amasa missed a deadline to gather Judah's troops, Joab stabbed him to death while greeting him at Gibeon.

details.label: Family
details.value: Son of Abigail and Jether the Ishmaelite; nephew of David

events.title: Receives command of Absalom's army
Receives David's promise of command in Joab's place
Misses David's three-day deadline to gather Judah
Is stabbed to death by Joab at Gibeon

label: Amaziah
overview: Amaziah ruled Judah for twenty-nine years after his father Joash. He defeated Edom, then worshiped its gods and rejected a prophet's warning. Jehoash of Israel captured him in battle, and conspirators later killed him at Lachish.

card.role: King of Judah, son of Joash

details.label: Role
details.value: King of Judah for twenty-nine years, beginning at age twenty-five

details.label: Family
details.value: Son of Joash and Jehoaddan; father of Azariah

details.label: Buried
details.value: With his fathers in the City of David, Jerusalem

events.title: Executes his father's murderers but spares their sons according to the Law
Dismisses his hired Israelite troops after a man of God warns him
Defeats Edom; his army throws ten thousand captives off a cliff
Worships Edom's gods and threatens the prophet who rebukes him
Rejects Jehoash's warning and is captured as God judges Judah's idolatry
Flees conspirators to Lachish, where they kill him

label: Ammon
overview: Ammon was the son of Lot, born through an incestuous union with his younger daughter following the destruction of Sodom. He became the ancestral father of the Ammonites, a nation that settled east of the Jordan River in the plateau of the Transjordan. Throughout biblical history, the Ammonites were frequent adversaries of Israel, often joining forces with other nations like Moab or the Philistines to oppress the Israelites during the period of the Judges and the Monarchy. Despite their shared heritage with Abraham, the Ammonites were noted for their worship of the god Molech and were eventually excluded from the assembly of the Lord. The story of Ammon serves as a tragic footnote to the life of Lot and the origin of a persistent enemy of God’s people.

events.title: Origin in the Cave
events.summary: Ammon is born to Lot’s younger daughter in a cave near Zoar after the flight from Sodom.
developments: The daughters of Lot believe no men are left on earth to marry (Genesis 19:31)
They intoxicate their father to preserve their lineage (Genesis 19:32-35)
The younger daughter gives birth to a son named Ben-ammi (Genesis 19:38)
The name Ben-ammi means 'son of my people' (Genesis 19:38)
events.significance: His birth establishes a kinship between the Ammonites and the Israelites.

events.title: Granting of Territory
events.summary: God identifies the land of the Ammonites as a specific inheritance he gave to the descendants of Lot.
developments: Israel is commanded not to harass the Ammonites or contend with them (Deuteronomy 2:19)
The land of Ar is identified as their possession (Deuteronomy 2:19)
They had dispossessed a race of giants known as the Zamzummim (Deuteronomy 2:20-21)
God acknowledges their rights to the land based on their ancestry (Deuteronomy 2:19)
events.significance: This shows God's sovereign distribution of land to nations other than Israel.

events.title: Early Oppression of Israel
events.summary: The Ammonites join Eglon of Moab to attack and occupy parts of Israel.
developments: Eglon gathers the Ammonites and Amalekites to his side (Judges 3:13)
They defeat Israel and take possession of the City of Palms (Judges 3:13)
Israel serves Eglon for eighteen years (Judges 3:14)
The alliance marks the beginning of frequent Ammonite incursion (Judges 3:13)
events.significance: Ammon becomes a recurring tool of divine discipline against Israelite idolatry.

events.title: The War with Jephthah
events.summary: The Ammonites claim Israel stole their land, leading to a major conflict led by Jephthah.
developments: Ammonites make war on Israel for eighteen years (Judges 10:8)
The King of Ammon demands the return of land from the Arnon to the Jabbok (Judges 11:13)
Jephthah argues that God gave the land to Israel through the defeat of Sihon (Judges 11:21-24)
Jephthah decisively defeats the Ammonites from Aroer to Minnith (Judges 11:32-33)
events.significance: This established the legal and historical borders between the two nations.

events.title: The Siege of Jabesh-gilead
events.summary: Nahash the Ammonite threatens to gouge out the right eyes of Israelite men, sparking Saul's first victory.
developments: Nahash encamps against Jabesh-gilead and demands a cruel treaty (1 Samuel 11:1-2)
Saul is filled with the Spirit and musters an army of 330,000 (1 Samuel 11:6-8)
Israel strikes the Ammonite camp until the heat of the day (1 Samuel 11:11)
The survivors are scattered so that no two are left together (1 Samuel 11:11)
events.significance: This victory confirmed Saul's kingship in the eyes of the people.

events.title: The War of the Insult
events.summary: King Hanun of Ammon insults David’s ambassadors, leading to a war that results in the fall of Rabbah.
developments: Hanun shaves the beards and cuts the garments of David's messengers (2 Samuel 10:4)
Ammon hires Syrian mercenaries to fight David's army (2 Samuel 10:6)
Joab and Abishai defeat the combined forces (2 Samuel 10:9-14)
David eventually captures the capital, Rabbah, and its royal crown (2 Samuel 12:26-31)
events.significance: This war was the backdrop for David's sin with Bathsheba and the height of his empire.

events.title: Solomon's Spiritual Compromise
events.summary: Solomon marries Ammonite women who lead him into the worship of their gods.
developments: Solomon loves many foreign women, including Ammonites (1 Kings 11:1)
He builds a high place for Molech, the abomination of the Ammonites (1 Kings 11:7)
Rehoboam's mother is identified as Naamah the Ammonitess (1 Kings 14:21)
This idolatry leads to the eventual tearing away of the kingdom (1 Kings 11:11)
events.significance: The influence of Ammon reached the very heart of the Jerusalem Temple.

events.title: Opposition to the Wall
events.summary: Tobiah the Ammonite attempts to stop the reconstruction of Jerusalem's walls after the exile.
developments: Tobiah mocks the strength of the wall, saying a fox could break it (Nehemiah 4:3)
The Ammonites conspire to fight against Jerusalem to cause confusion (Nehemiah 4:7-8)
Nehemiah arms the builders to defend against the threat (Nehemiah 4:13-18)
The wall is finished despite the Ammonite pressure (Nehemiah 6:15-16)
events.significance: The ancient enmity persisted even after the return from Babylonian captivity.

label: Amnon
overview: David's firstborn son, born to Ahinoam in Hebron. He pretended to be ill, raped his sister Tamar and then had her thrown out. Two years later, Absalom ordered his servants to kill him at a sheepshearing feast.

details.label: Family
details.value: Firstborn son of David, by Ahinoam of Jezreel

events.title: Follows Jonadab's advice, rapes Tamar and has her thrown out
Absalom's servants kill him at a feast two years later

label: Amon
overview: Ruled Judah for two years and worshiped the idols his father Manasseh had served. He did not humble himself before the LORD. His servants killed him in his house, and the people made his son Josiah king.

details.label: Role
details.value: King in Jerusalem for two years, beginning at twenty-two

details.label: Buried
details.value: His tomb in the garden of Uzza

events.title: Becomes king and serves his father's idols
Is killed by his servants in his house
The people kill the conspirators and make his son Josiah king

label: Amos
overview: A sheepherder from Tekoa whom God sent to prophesy to Israel. He condemned oppression of the poor, called for justice and righteousness, and announced judgment and restoration.

details.label: Role
details.value: Herdsman and tender of sycamore-fig trees, sent to prophesy

details.label: Named in
details.value: Prophecy during the reigns of Uzziah and Jeroboam son of Jehoash

events.title: God takes him from tending the flock to prophesy to Israel
Condemns oppression and calls for justice and righteousness
Pleads for Israel during visions of judgment
Answers Amaziah's opposition with God's word of judgment
Announces God's promise to restore David's fallen tent and His people

label: Ananias
overview: Ananias is the name of three distinct and significant men in the New Testament. The first was a member of the early Jerusalem church who, along with his wife Sapphira, was struck dead for lying to the Holy Spirit about a financial gift. The second was a faithful disciple in Damascus whom God used to restore the sight of Saul of Tarsus and baptize him following his conversion. The third was a Jewish High Priest in Jerusalem who presided over the council during Paul's trial and was known for his harshness and political maneuvering. These figures represent three different facets of the early church's environment: internal discipline, external mission, and religious opposition.

events.title: The Lie of the Jerusalem Member
events.summary: Ananias and Sapphira attempt to deceive the apostles regarding the sale of their property.
developments: Ananias sells a piece of property (Acts 5:1)
He keeps back part of the proceeds with his wife's knowledge (Acts 5:2)
He brings only a portion and lays it at the apostles' feet as if it were the total (Acts 5:2)
Peter asks why Satan has filled his heart to lie to the Holy Spirit (Acts 5:3)
events.significance: This event established the absolute necessity of integrity within the early Christian community.

events.title: Judgment and Fear
events.summary: Ananias falls dead immediately after his deception is exposed by Peter.
developments: Ananias hears Peter's words and falls down dead (Acts 5:5)
Great fear comes upon all who hear of it (Acts 5:5)
Young men wrap him up, carry him out, and bury him (Acts 5:6)
His wife suffers the same fate three hours later (Acts 5:7-10)
events.significance: The severity of the judgment highlighted God's holiness in the infancy of the church.

events.title: The Vision in Damascus
events.summary: The second Ananias receives a divine command to find the blinded Saul of Tarsus.
developments: The Lord speaks to Ananias in a vision (Acts 9:10)
He is told to go to the house of Judas on 'Straight Street' (Acts 9:11)
Ananias expresses fear because of Saul's reputation for persecution (Acts 9:13-14)
The Lord identifies Saul as a 'chosen instrument' (Acts 9:15)
events.significance: Ananias' obedience was a critical link in the conversion of the Apostle Paul.

events.title: Healing and Baptism of Saul
events.summary: Ananias lays hands on Saul, restoring his sight and welcoming him into the faith.
developments: He enters the house and calls him 'Brother Saul' (Acts 9:17)
Something like scales fall from Saul's eyes (Acts 9:18)
Saul regains his sight and is baptized by Ananias (Acts 9:18)
In Paul's later defense, he calls Ananias a 'devout man according to the law' (Acts 22:12)
events.significance: Ananias represents the grace of the church in accepting a former enemy.

events.title: The High Priest’s Cruelty
events.summary: The third Ananias, the High Priest, orders Paul to be struck during his trial.
developments: Paul looks at the council and declares his good conscience (Acts 23:1)
Ananias commands those near Paul to strike him on the mouth (Acts 23:2)
Paul calls him a 'whitewashed wall' for breaking the law while judging (Acts 23:3)
Paul later apologizes for the insult, not knowing he was the High Priest (Acts 23:5)
events.significance: This Ananias illustrates the corruption of the religious leadership in Jerusalem.

events.title: The Prosecution of Paul
events.summary: Ananias travels to Caesarea to personally lead the legal case against Paul before Felix.
developments: He goes down after five days with some elders and a lawyer named Tertullus (Acts 24:1)
They present their case against Paul to the governor (Acts 24:1)
They accuse Paul of being a ringleader of a sect and a disturber of the peace (Acts 24:5)
The high priest's presence shows the level of institutional desire to silence Paul (Acts 24:1-9)
events.significance: Ananias’ persistent opposition forced Paul's case into the Roman legal system.

label: Andrew
overview: Fisherman from Bethsaida and brother of Simon Peter. He followed Jesus after hearing John the Baptist call Him the Lamb of God, then brought Peter to Him. He later pointed out a boy with five loaves and two fish.

details.label: Role
details.value: Fisherman and one of the twelve apostles

events.title: Follows Jesus and brings his brother Simon to Him
Leaves his fishing nets when Jesus calls
Points out a boy with five barley loaves and two fish
Joins Philip in telling Jesus that Greeks want to see Him

label: Anna
overview: Prophetess from the tribe of Asher who worshiped at the temple with fasting and prayer. Widowed and eighty-four years old, she thanked God for the child Jesus and spoke about Him to those awaiting Jerusalem's redemption.

details.label: Role
details.value: Prophetess who worshiped with fasting and prayer

details.label: Family
details.value: Daughter of Phanuel, of Asher's tribe; married for seven years before widowhood

label: Annas
overview: A high priest and Caiaphas's father-in-law, Annas received Jesus after His arrest and sent Him bound to Caiaphas. He later gathered with the authorities who questioned Peter and John about a healing.

events.title: Receives Jesus after His arrest and sends Him bound to Caiaphas
Gathers with the authorities who question Peter and John

label: Apollos
overview: An eloquent Jewish teacher from Alexandria who taught about Jesus. Priscilla and Aquila explained God's way to him more accurately, and he went to Achaia, helping believers and showing from Scripture that Jesus was the Christ.

details.label: Role
details.value: Eloquent teacher well versed in the Scriptures

events.title: Teaches in Ephesus and receives further instruction from Priscilla and Aquila
Helps believers in Achaia and proves from Scripture that Jesus is the Christ
Declines an immediate visit to Corinth despite Paul's urging

label: Aquila
overview: Worked as a tentmaker with his wife Priscilla and Paul in Corinth. A Jew from Pontus, he traveled with them to Ephesus, where the couple instructed Apollos. Paul called them fellow workers who had risked their lives for him.

details.label: Role
details.value: Tentmaker; fellow worker in Christ Jesus

events.title: Meets Paul in Corinth after leaving Italy with Priscilla
Travels with Paul and Priscilla to Ephesus
Explains God's way more accurately to Apollos with Priscilla
Paul greets him and Priscilla and the church meeting in their house

label: Aram
overview: Aram was the grandson of Noah and a son of Shem, positioned as the ancestral patriarch of the Aramean people. His descendants settled in the region that would eventually become known as Syria, with the Aramaic language becoming a dominant tongue in the ancient Near East for centuries. In biblical geography, the land of Aram encompassed a wide area of the Fertile Crescent, including regions like Aram-naharaim and Aram-damascus. The patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob all had deep familial roots in Aram, often returning there to find wives and maintain tribal connections. While Aram’s personal life is recorded primarily in genealogies, his legacy shaped the cultural and linguistic landscape of the biblical world.

events.title: Post-Flood Lineage
events.summary: Aram is listed in the Table of Nations as a primary descendant of Shem.
developments: He is recorded as one of the five sons of Shem (Genesis 10:22)
His brothers include Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, and Lud (Genesis 10:22)
Aram becomes the father of Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash (Genesis 10:23)
This genealogy places him at the foundation of the post-diluvian world (Genesis 10:1-32)
events.significance: Aram is established as the progenitor of a major ethnic and linguistic group.

events.title: The Family of Nahor
events.summary: A different Aram appears in the line of Abraham's brother, Nahor.
developments: Abraham receives news of his brother Nahor's family (Genesis 22:20)
Kemuel is identified as the father of Aram (Genesis 22:21)
This Aram is the nephew of Bethuel, the father of Rebekah (Genesis 22:22-23)
The name continues to be prominent within the ancestral homeland (Genesis 22:21)
events.significance: The name's repetition reinforces the strong tie between the Hebrews and Arameans.

events.title: The Homeland of the Matriarchs
events.summary: The land associated with Aram becomes the source of wives for the patriarchs.
developments: Abraham's servant goes to Aram-naharaim to find a wife for Isaac (Genesis 24:10)
Isaac marries Rebekah, the daughter of Bethuel the Aramean (Genesis 25:20)
Laban, the brother of Rebekah, is consistently called an Aramean (Genesis 25:20)
Jacob later flees to the land of the people of the east in Aram (Genesis 28:5)
events.significance: Aram serves as the genetic and cultural reservoir for the family of promise.

events.title: The Aramean Ancestor
events.summary: The Israelites are commanded to recite a liturgy identifying their ancestor as a wandering Aramean.
developments: The worshipper must say, 'A wandering Aramean was my father' (Deuteronomy 26:5)
This refers to Jacob's long residence and family formation in Aram (Deuteronomy 26:5)
The confession recalls the descent into Egypt from that state (Deuteronomy 26:5)
It acknowledges Israel's humble and foreign origins (Deuteronomy 26:5)
events.significance: Aram is formally recognized as the starting point of Israel's national journey.

events.title: The First Oppressor
events.summary: The land of Aram provides the first foreign king to oppress Israel after the conquest.
developments: Cushan-rishathaim, king of Aram-naharaim, subjugates Israel (Judges 3:8)
Israel serves him for eight years (Judges 3:8)
The Lord raises up Othniel to deliver the people from the Aramean king (Judges 3:9-10)
The Spirit of the Lord enables Othniel to prevail against Aram (Judges 3:10)
events.significance: Aram shifts from a place of kinship to a source of divine discipline.

events.title: Conquest by David
events.summary: King David defeats the Aramean kingdoms and makes them tribute-paying vassals.
developments: David defeats Hadadezer king of Zobah, an Aramean state (2 Samuel 8:3)
Arameans of Damascus come to help but are also defeated (2 Samuel 8:5)
David puts garrisons in Aram of Damascus (2 Samuel 8:6)
Aram becomes a servant to David, bringing tribute to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 8:6)
events.significance: This marks the peak of Israelite political dominance over the land of Aram.

events.title: The Rise of Damascus
events.summary: Following Solomon's reign, Aram-damascus emerges as a major rival to Israel.
developments: Rezon son of Eliada seizes Damascus and becomes an adversary (1 Kings 11:23-25)
The Arameans reign in Damascus and trouble Israel for generations (1 Kings 11:25)
King Asa of Judah hires Ben-hadad of Aram to attack Israel (1 Kings 15:18-20)
Aram becomes a significant 'buffer state' in regional politics (1 Kings 15:20)
events.significance: Aram transitions into a primary and persistent military threat to the northern kingdom.

events.title: Genealogy of Jesus
events.summary: Aram (Ram) is listed in the direct lineage of the Messiah.
developments: Aram is listed as the son of Hezron (Matthew 1:3)
He is the father of Amminadab (Matthew 1:4)
This individual is part of the line from Judah to David (Matthew 1:3-6)
The name is also rendered as 'Ram' in the Old Testament records (1 Chronicles 2:9-10)
events.significance: The name persists in the central redemptive line of the New Testament.

label: Arameans
overview: The Arameans were a group of Semitic tribes and kingdoms descended from Aram, primarily occupying the regions of modern-day Syria and Upper Mesopotamia. Throughout the Old Testament, they were significant neighbors, rivals, and relatives of the Israelites. The Hebrew patriarchs identified themselves as having Aramean roots, but by the time of the Monarchy, the Arameans of Damascus became frequent military adversaries. Their language, Aramaic, eventually became the lingua franca of the Near East, spoken by Jews during the exile and by Jesus and His disciples in the New Testament. The Arameans represent the complex interplay of shared ancestry and persistent national conflict in the ancient biblical world.

events.title: The Aramean Matriarchs
events.summary: The mothers of the Israelite tribes are drawn from the Aramean household of Laban.
developments: Rebekah is the daughter of Bethuel the Aramean (Genesis 25:20)
Laban is consistently identified as the Aramean from Paddan-aram (Genesis 25:20)
Leah and Rachel are the daughters of Laban the Aramean (Genesis 29:16)
Jacob lives and works in the Aramean territory for twenty years (Genesis 31:41)
events.significance: The Arameans are the closest ethnic relatives to the chosen family of Israel.

events.title: Boundary Covenant
events.summary: Jacob and Laban establish a heap of stones as a permanent border between the Hebrews and Arameans.
developments: Laban calls the heap 'Jegar-sahadutha' in Aramaic (Genesis 31:47)
Jacob calls the heap 'Galeed' in Hebrew (Genesis 31:47)
They swear not to pass the heap to do one another harm (Genesis 31:52)
The covenant recognizes the distinct linguistic and national identities of the two groups (Genesis 31:47-53)
events.significance: This marks the formal separation of the two kindred peoples into different nations.

events.title: The Coalition against David
events.summary: The Arameans act as mercenaries for the Ammonites to fight against King David.
developments: Ammonites hire 20,000 Aramean foot soldiers from Beth-rehob and Zobah (2 Samuel 10:6)
They also hire 12,000 men from the land of Tob (2 Samuel 10:6)
Joab and the Israelite army defeat the Aramean coalition (2 Samuel 10:13-14)
The Arameans subsequently fear to help the Ammonites again (2 Samuel 10:19)
events.significance: This conflict established David's superiority over the northern regional powers.

events.title: Naaman the Aramean
events.summary: A high-ranking Aramean commander seeks healing from the God of Israel.
developments: Naaman is the commander of the army of the king of Syria/Aram (2 Kings 5:1)
He is a leper who hears of the prophet Elisha (2 Kings 5:2-3)
He washes in the Jordan River and is cured (2 Kings 5:14)
He declares there is no God in all the earth but in Israel (2 Kings 5:15)
events.significance: Naaman’s conversion showed that God's grace extended even to Israel's national enemies.

events.title: The Blinded Army
events.summary: God supernaturally protects Elisha from an Aramean raiding party.
developments: The king of Aram sends horses and chariots to surround Dothan (2 Kings 6:14)
Elisha prays and the Lord strikes the Arameans with blindness (2 Kings 6:18)
Elisha leads the blinded army into the heart of Samaria (2 Kings 6:19-20)
The king of Israel feeds them and sends them home in peace (2 Kings 6:22-23)
events.significance: The event demonstrated that Aramean military might was useless against divine protection.

events.title: The Abandoned Camp
events.summary: During a famine in Samaria, God causes the Aramean army to flee in terror without a fight.
developments: The Arameans hear the sound of a great army of chariots and horses (2 Kings 7:6)
They believe Israel has hired Hittite and Egyptian mercenaries (2 Kings 7:6)
They flee at twilight, leaving their tents and provisions behind (2 Kings 7:7)
Four lepers discover the empty camp and find food for the city (2 Kings 7:8-11)
events.significance: God used the Arameans’ own fear to provide for His starving people.

events.title: The Fall of Damascus
events.summary: The Aramean kingdom of Damascus is ultimately destroyed by the Assyrian Empire.
developments: Rezin of Aram and Pekah of Israel attack Jerusalem (2 Kings 16:5)
Ahaz of Judah hires Tiglath-pileser of Assyria to help (2 Kings 16:7)
Assyria captures Damascus and carries the people into exile at Kir (2 Kings 16:9)
Rezin is killed, ending the independent Aramean power in Damascus (2 Kings 16:9)
events.significance: The collapse of Aram removed the northern shield for Israel against Assyria.

events.title: The Language of the Exile
events.summary: Aramaic becomes the primary administrative and common language of the post-exilic world.
developments: Sections of Ezra and Daniel are written in Aramaic (Daniel 2:4-7:28)
The Persian Empire uses 'Aramaic' for official decrees (Ezra 4:7)
The returning Jews bring the language back to Israel (Nehemiah 8:8)
The New Testament preserves Aramaic phrases like 'Talitha cumi' and 'Abba' (Mark 5:41, 14:36)
events.significance: Though the nation fell, the Aramean language became the vehicle for later Scripture.

label: Araunah
overview: Jebusite who sold David his threshing floor for an altar during a plague. He offered the oxen and equipment for free, but David insisted on paying. Solomon later built the temple on that site.

card.role: Jebusite who sold David his land

label: Aristarchus
overview: Traveled with Paul and came from Thessalonica in Macedonia. A crowd seized him during the riot at Ephesus, and he later sailed with Paul toward Italy. Paul called him a fellow prisoner and fellow worker.

details.label: Role
details.value: Fellow prisoner and fellow worker of Paul

events.title: The crowd seizes him during the riot at Ephesus
Goes ahead with Paul's companions to wait at Troas
Sails with Paul on the journey to Italy
Paul sends his greetings and calls him a fellow prisoner

label: Artaxerxes
overview: King of Persia who authorized Ezra's mission and allowed Nehemiah to rebuild Jerusalem. Ezra also records his order to stop rebuilding the city after opponents sent accusations against it.

card.role: Persian king in Ezra and Nehemiah

events.title: Orders Jerusalem's rebuilding stopped after receiving accusations
Authorizes Ezra's mission with offerings, supplies, and authority to appoint judges
Grants Nehemiah leave, letters, timber, and an escort for Jerusalem

label: Asa
overview: Ruled Judah for forty-one years and removed idols. He relied on God against the Cushites, but later relied on Aram, imprisoned the seer who rebuked him, and sought physicians alone when his feet became diseased.

details.label: Role
details.value: King of Judah for forty-one years

details.label: Buried
details.value: His own tomb in the City of David

events.title: Becomes king and removes his fathers' idols
Calls on God and defeats Zerah's Cushite army
Renews the covenant and removes Maacah as queen mother
Buys Aram's help against Baasha and is rebuked for relying on Aram
Imprisons Hanani and oppresses some of the people
Seeks physicians rather than the LORD during illness, then dies

label: Asahel
overview: One of David's Thirty and a son of Zeruiah, known for his speed. He chased Abner despite repeated warnings, and Abner killed him with the butt of his spear.

details.label: Role

details.label: Family

events.title: Pursues Abner despite his warnings and is killed
Is buried in his father's tomb at Bethlehem

card.role: David's chief musician before the ark

details.label: Role
details.value: Chief musician before the ark; seer

details.label: Family
details.value: Son of Berechiah, descended from Gershom and Levi

events.title: Is appointed to play bronze cymbals with Heman and Ethan
Leads worship before the ark and receives David's song of thanksgiving
Directs his sons as they prophesy with musical instruments

label: Asher
overview: Son of Jacob and Zilpah, named by Leah after she expressed her happiness at his birth. Jacob's blessing said Asher would have rich food and provide royal delicacies.

details.label: Family

details.label: Family
details.value: Father of Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah and Serah

label: Ashpenaz
overview: Nebuchadnezzar's chief court official, ordered to select and train young Israelites for royal service. God gave Daniel favor with him, but he feared the king would kill him if Daniel's diet left him looking thinner.

details.label: Role
details.value: Chief of the king's court officials

label: Athaliah
overview: Ruled Judah for six years after her son Ahaziah died. She murdered the royal heirs, but Joash was hidden from her. When Jehoiada made Joash king, she cried treason and was taken outside the temple and killed.

details.label: Family
details.value: Granddaughter of Omri; mother of Ahaziah

events.title: Counsels her son Ahaziah in wickedness
Murders the royal heirs and rules while Joash remains hidden
Cries treason at Joash's coronation and is taken outside the temple and killed

label: Augustus
overview: Issued the decree for an empire-wide census in Luke's account of Jesus' birth. Joseph went from Nazareth to Bethlehem to register with Mary, who was pregnant, and Jesus was born while they were there.

card.role: Roman emperor who ordered the census

label: Azariah
overview: Azariah is a prominent name in Scripture, most notably referring to King Uzziah of Judah and one of the three Hebrew youths in Babylon. As King of Judah, Azariah enjoyed a long and prosperous fifty-two-year reign, becoming a powerful military leader and innovator until his pride led him to usurp the priestly role in the Temple, resulting in lifelong leprosy. In the book of Daniel, another Azariah (renamed Abednego) demonstrated unwavering faith by refusing to bow to a golden image and surviving a fiery furnace. Additionally, the name is associated with several high priests and prophets who challenged various kings to return to the worship of God.

events.title: Ascension to the Throne
events.summary: Azariah (Uzziah) begins his reign in Jerusalem at age sixteen, following the death of his father Amaziah.
developments: He is made king by the people of Judah (2 Kings 14:21)
He begins reigning in the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam II of Israel (2 Kings 15:1)
His mother is Jecoliah of Jerusalem (2 Kings 15:2)
He reigns for fifty-two years in total (2 Kings 15:2)
events.significance: His long reign brought a period of significant stability to the southern kingdom.

events.title: Military and Civil Success
events.summary: Azariah strengthens Judah's defenses and economy through military innovation and agricultural development.
developments: He defeats the Philistines and breaks down the walls of Gath and Ashdod (2 Chronicles 26:6)
He builds towers in Jerusalem and in the wilderness (2 Chronicles 26:9-10)
He equips a massive army with shields, spears, and helmets (2 Chronicles 26:14)
He installs engines on the towers to shoot arrows and large stones (2 Chronicles 26:15)
events.significance: Under Azariah, Judah reached a level of power not seen since the days of Solomon.

events.title: The Sin of Presumption
events.summary: Filled with pride, Azariah enters the Temple to perform a task reserved only for the priests.
developments: When he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction (2 Chronicles 26:16)
He enters the Temple to burn incense on the altar of incense (2 Chronicles 26:16)
Azariah the priest and eighty other courageous priests oppose him (2 Chronicles 26:17-18)
The king becomes angry with the priests while holding the censer (2 Chronicles 26:19)
events.significance: This moment illustrates the boundary between civil and religious authority in Israel.

events.title: Judgment of Leprosy
events.summary: God strikes Azariah with leprosy immediately as he stands in his pride within the holy place.
developments: Leprosy breaks out on his forehead in the presence of the priests (2 Chronicles 26:19)
The priests hurry him out of the Temple (2 Chronicles 26:20)
He himself hastens to go out because the Lord had struck him (2 Chronicles 26:20)
He remains a leper until the day of his death (2 Chronicles 26:21)
events.significance: The king's external defilement reflected his internal spiritual rebellion.

events.title: Exile and Death
events.summary: Azariah lives in a separate house and is excluded from the royal tombs at his burial.
developments: He dwells in a separate house, being excluded from the house of the Lord (2 Chronicles 26:21)
His son Jotham governs the palace and judges the people in his place (2 Chronicles 26:21)
He is buried with his fathers in the burial field belonging to the kings (2 Chronicles 26:23)
They do not put him in the tombs because 'He is a leper' (2 Chronicles 26:23)
events.significance: His life ended in isolation, serving as a permanent warning against royal arrogance.

events.title: Exile of the Hebrew Youth
events.summary: A different Azariah is taken as a noble captive to Babylon and renamed Abednego.
developments: He is chosen for his intelligence and lack of blemish (Daniel 1:3-4)
The chief of the eunuchs gives him the name Abednego (Daniel 1:7)
He resolves not to defile himself with the king's food (Daniel 1:8)
After ten days of vegetables and water, he looks better than the others (Daniel 1:15)
events.significance: This Azariah represents the faithful remnant in the midst of a pagan culture.

events.title: The Fiery Furnace
events.summary: Azariah (Abednego) refuses to worship the golden image and is protected by God in the fire.
developments: He and his friends refuse to bow to Nebuchadnezzar's idol (Daniel 3:12)
They are thrown into the seven-times-heated furnace (Daniel 3:19-23)
A fourth person, like a 'son of the gods,' is seen in the fire with them (Daniel 3:25)
They emerge from the fire without even the smell of smoke (Daniel 3:27)
events.significance: His deliverance forced the Babylonian king to acknowledge the power of the true God.

events.title: The Prophet's Warning
events.summary: A prophet named Azariah son of Oded encourages King Asa to seek the Lord.
developments: The Spirit of God comes upon Azariah (2 Chronicles 15:1)
He meets Asa and says, 'The Lord is with you while you are with him' (2 Chronicles 15:2)
He urges the king to be strong and not let his hands be weak (2 Chronicles 15:7)
His words spark a major religious reform in Judah (2 Chronicles 15:8-15)
events.significance: Azariah the prophet served as the catalyst for one of Judah's greatest spiritual revivals.

overview: Captain of a raiding band under Ish-bosheth. He and his brother Rechab murdered Ish-bosheth in bed and brought his head to David. David condemned the murder of a righteous man and had both brothers executed.

The Holy Spirit sends him and Saul to preach in Cyprus

Receives Jeremiah's field deeds with instructions to preserve them in a clay jar
Is accused of influencing Jeremiah and taken with him to Egypt

The LORD strikes her child, who dies as Nathan foretold

Reminds David of his oath that Solomon will succeed him
Asks Solomon to give Abishag to Adonijah; Solomon orders Adonijah's death

Daniel announces God's judgment on his pride and kingdom
Honors Daniel but is killed that night; Darius receives the kingdom

label: Ben-hadad
overview: Ben-hadad was the name of several powerful kings of Aram-Damascus who were significant adversaries and, at times, reluctant allies of the kings of Israel. The most prominent Ben-hadad engaged in multiple wars with King Ahab, leading a massive coalition of thirty-two kings to besiege Samaria before being twice defeated by Israel. Despite his arrogance, he was forced to plead for his life in sackcloth and ashes. Later, his house was cursed by the prophet Elisha, who predicted his murder by Hazael. The various Ben-hadads represent the persistent threat of the Aramean Empire and the complex international politics that defined the era of the divided kingdom.

events.title: Alliance with King Asa
events.summary: King Asa of Judah hires Ben-hadad to break his treaty with Israel and attack from the north.
developments: Asa sends silver and gold from the Temple as a bribe (1 Kings 15:18)
Ben-hadad listens to Asa and attacks Ijon, Dan, and Abel-beth-maacah (1 Kings 15:20)
This forces King Baasha of Israel to abandon his blockade of Judah (1 Kings 15:21)
Ben-hadad is identified as the son of Tabrimmon (1 Kings 15:18)
events.significance: This event established the pattern of the Arameans acting as a paid third-party in Hebrew civil wars.

events.title: The Siege of Samaria
events.summary: Ben-hadad leads a massive coalition of thirty-two kings to demand the surrender of Ahab’s capital.
developments: He demands Ahab's silver, gold, wives, and children (1 Kings 20:3)
Ahab initially complies but refuses a second, more intrusive demand (1 Kings 20:4-9)
Ben-hadad boasts that the dust of Samaria will not suffice for his army's hands (1 Kings 20:10)
A prophet tells Ahab that God will deliver the multitude to him (1 Kings 20:13)
events.significance: His arrogance set the stage for a humiliating defeat that proved God's power over superior numbers.

events.title: Defeat at the Hills and Plain
events.summary: Aramean advisors wrongly believe Israel's God is only a god of the hills, leading to a second disaster.
developments: They decide to fight on the plain where they think they will be stronger (1 Kings 20:23-25)
The Arameans fill the country while the Israelites look like two little flocks of goats (1 Kings 20:27)
Israel slaughters 100,000 Aramean foot soldiers in one day (1 Kings 20:29)
A wall in Aphek falls on 27,000 of the survivors (1 Kings 20:30)
events.significance: The victory vindicated God's glory as the Lord of all geography, not just localized regions.

events.title: The Mercy of Ahab
events.summary: Ben-hadad surrenders in sackcloth and receives a treaty from Ahab instead of execution.
developments: Ben-hadad hides in an inner chamber in the city (1 Kings 20:30)
His servants approach Ahab wearing sackcloth and ropes on their heads (1 Kings 20:32)
Ahab calls him 'my brother' and lets him into his chariot (1 Kings 20:33)
A prophet rebukes Ahab, saying his life shall go for Ben-hadad's life (1 Kings 20:42)
events.significance: Ahab's misplaced leniency toward a condemned enemy brought judgment upon himself.

events.title: The Siege and the Famine
events.summary: Ben-hadad returns years later to besiege Samaria, causing a catastrophic famine.
developments: The siege is so severe that mothers resort to cannibalism (2 Kings 6:24-29)
Elisha predicts that food will be plentiful by the next day (2 Kings 7:1)
God causes the Arameans to hear the noise of a great army (2 Kings 7:6)
The Aramean army flees at twilight, leaving all their supplies behind (2 Kings 7:7)
events.significance: God delivered Israel from Ben-hadad through supernatural psychological warfare.

events.title: Illness and Elisha’s Visit
events.summary: While sick, Ben-hadad sends Hazael to Elisha to inquire if he will recover.
developments: The king of Aram is told the 'man of God' has come to Damascus (2 Kings 8:7)
He sends forty camel-loads of every good thing of Damascus as a gift (2 Kings 8:9)
Elisha tells Hazael that the king could recover, but will certainly die (2 Kings 8:10)
Elisha weeps because he sees the evil Hazael will do to Israel (2 Kings 8:11-12)
events.significance: The prophecy marked the end of the line of Ben-hadad and the rise of a more brutal Aramean king.

events.title: Murder and Usurpation
events.summary: Hazael returns to the palace and suffocates the king to take the throne.
developments: Hazael tells Ben-hadad that the prophet said he would recover (2 Kings 8:14)
The next day, Hazael takes a thick cloth, dips it in water, and spreads it on the king's face (2 Kings 8:15)
Ben-hadad dies of suffocation (2 Kings 8:15)
Hazael reigns in his place over Aram-Damascus (2 Kings 8:15)
events.significance: The assassination fulfilled Elisha's word and began a new era of Aramean aggression.

events.title: The Next Ben-hadad
events.summary: The son of Hazael, also named Ben-hadad, loses territory back to Israel.
developments: He succeeds Hazael as king of Aram (2 Kings 13:24)
Jehoash of Israel defeats him three times in battle (2 Kings 13:25)
Israel recovers the cities that Hazael had taken from them (2 Kings 13:25)
This fulfilled the prophecy of the dying Elisha (2 Kings 13:14-19)
events.significance: The name Ben-hadad continued as a symbol of the shifting power balance between the two nations.

label: Benaiah

David appoints him over his guard
Helps escort Solomon to Gihon to be anointed king

Kills Joab at the sanctuary and takes his place over the army
Kills Shimei at Solomon's command

Constructs the ark from acacia wood

Marries Ruth, who gives birth to Obed

label: Brothers
overview: In the biblical narrative, the 'brothers' of Jesus are mentioned as part of His immediate family, consisting of James, Joses, Simon, and Judas, along with unnamed sisters. Initially, they are depicted as skeptical of Jesus' ministry, even attempting to restrain Him during His public work and urging Him to seek fame in Jerusalem. However, this dynamic changed fundamentally after the resurrection. James and Jude became prominent leaders in the early church and authors of New Testament epistles. The journey of the brothers from family skeptics to devoted 'servants of the Lord' serves as a powerful testament to the transformative reality of Christ’s resurrection.

events.title: Named in Nazareth
events.summary: The citizens of Nazareth identify Jesus' brothers by name during a visit to the synagogue.
developments: The townspeople ask, 'Is not this the carpenter's son?' (Matthew 13:55)
His mother is called Mary (Matthew 13:55)
His brothers are named James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas (Matthew 13:55)
His sisters are also noted as being present with them (Matthew 13:56)
events.significance: This provides the primary historical list of Jesus' immediate siblings.

events.title: Attempt to Restrain Jesus
events.summary: Concerned for His well-being or reputation, Jesus' family attempts to take Him home.
developments: His family hears about the massive crowds and says, 'He is out of his mind' (Mark 3:21)
His mother and brothers arrive and stand outside the house where He is teaching (Mark 3:31)
They send word to Him, calling for Him to come out (Mark 3:31)
Jesus defines His true family as those who do the will of God (Mark 3:33-35)
events.significance: The brothers' early opposition highlighted the division Jesus' mission caused within His own household.

events.title: Unbelief and Ridicule
events.summary: The brothers mock Jesus’ strategy and encourage Him to seek public attention in Judea.
developments: They tell Him to leave Galilee and go to Judea so His disciples can see His works (John 7:3)
They argue that no one works in secret if they want to be known (John 7:4)
The text explicitly states: 'For not even his brothers believed in him' (John 7:5)
Jesus tells them that His time has not yet come, while their time is always ready (John 7:6)
events.significance: Their skepticism was a major part of Jesus' personal burden during His earthly ministry.

events.title: Absence at the Cross
events.summary: Because His brothers do not yet believe, Jesus entrusts the care of His mother to the Apostle John.
developments: Jesus sees His mother and the disciple whom He loved standing nearby (John 19:26)
He says to Mary, 'Woman, behold, your son!' (John 19:26)
He says to John, 'Behold, your mother!' (John 19:27)
From that hour, John takes her into his own home (John 19:27)
events.significance: The lack of faith among the brothers had profound consequences for the family's structure.

events.title: United in Prayer
events.summary: Following the resurrection and ascension, the brothers are found among the core group of believers.
developments: The apostles return to Jerusalem and gather in the upper room (Acts 1:12-13)
They are devoting themselves to prayer with one accord (Acts 1:14)
The group includes the women and Mary the mother of Jesus (Acts 1:14)
The text specifically adds: 'and his brothers' (Acts 1:14)
events.significance: The resurrection had successfully converted the former skeptics into disciples.

events.title: The Appearance to James
events.summary: Paul records a specific resurrection appearance that likely catalyzed the brothers' faith.
developments: Paul lists the witnesses of the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 15:5-6)
He notes that Jesus 'appeared to James, then to all the apostles' (1 Corinthians 15:7)
This personal encounter with the brother of the Lord was a turning point (1 Corinthians 15:7)
It explains James’s rapid rise to leadership in the Jerusalem church (Galatians 1:19)
events.significance: The grace shown to a skeptical brother is a key element of the resurrection narrative.

events.title: Leadership of James
events.summary: James, the brother of the Lord, emerges as the primary leader of the Jerusalem church.
developments: Paul calls James one of the 'pillars' of the church (Galatians 2:9)
James presides over the Jerusalem Council regarding Gentile converts (Acts 15:13)
He delivers the final verdict on the requirements for Gentile believers (Acts 15:19-21)
He is a recognized authority figure even for Peter and Paul (Acts 21:18)
events.significance: The oldest brother moved from critic to the highest seat of early church governance.

events.title: The Letter of Jude
events.summary: Another brother, Jude, writes a General Epistle to the early Christian community.
developments: The author identifies himself as 'Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ' (Jude 1:1)
He also calls himself 'brother of James' (Jude 1:1)
He warns against false teachers who have crept in (Jude 1:4)
His letter becomes part of the New Testament canon (Jude 1:1-25)
events.significance: The brothers' legacy is preserved through their inspired contributions to Scripture.

label: Caiaphas
overview: High priest who urged that Jesus die for the nation. He accused Jesus of blasphemy at His hearing, and the council called for His death. He later joined the authorities who questioned Peter and John.

Chief priests and elders plot Jesus' arrest and death in his courtyard
Accuses Jesus of blasphemy, and the council declares Him deserving of death
Joins authorities who question Peter and John and forbid teaching in Jesus' name

overview: Worked the soil and brought an offering that God did not accept. He killed his brother Abel after God warned him about sin. God cursed him to wander but gave him a protective mark; he settled in Nod and built a city named for his son Enoch.

details.label: Family
details.value: Son of Adam and Eve; father of Enoch

events.title: Becomes angry when his offering is rejected, and God warns him about sin
Kills his brother Abel in a field
God curses him to wander and gives him a mark to protect him
Settles in Nod and builds a city named for his son Enoch

label: Caleb
overview: Judah's representative among the spies Moses sent into Canaan. He and Joshua urged Israel to trust the LORD and enter the land. At eighty-five, he received Hebron as his inheritance and drove out the sons of Anak.

details.label: Family

label: Candace
overview: Candace is the title or dynastic name used for the queens of Ethiopia (specifically the Kingdom of Kush) in the first century. In the Book of Acts, she is mentioned in connection with a high-ranking official of her court, the Ethiopian eunuch, who was the treasurer of her entire realm. This official had traveled to Jerusalem to worship and was reading the book of Isaiah when Philip the Evangelist encountered him. Through the conversion and baptism of this royal official, the influence of the gospel reached the highest levels of the Ethiopian court. Candace represents the sovereign authority of a distant African nation that became an early recipient of the Christian message.

events.title: The Queen of the Ethiopians
events.summary: Candace is identified as the reigning monarch of Ethiopia with a sophisticated court.
developments: She is explicitly called 'Candace, queen of the Ethiopians' (Acts 8:27)
Her kingdom was located south of Egypt in the region of Meroë (Acts 8:27)
She employed high-ranking officials to manage her vast wealth (Acts 8:27)
The term 'Candace' was a title like 'Pharaoh' or 'Caesar' (Acts 8:27)
events.significance: The mention of her name highlights the international reach of the early church's environment.

events.title: The Royal Treasurer's Mission
events.summary: The man in charge of all the queen's treasure travels to Jerusalem to seek the true God.
developments: An Ethiopian eunuch is introduced as a court official (Acts 8:27)
He was in charge of all her treasure (Acts 8:27)
He had come to Jerusalem to worship as a 'God-fearer' (Acts 8:27)
The queen allowed her highest financial officer to take a long pilgrimage (Acts 8:27-28)
events.significance: This illustrates the spiritual hunger present within the high courts of pagan nations.

events.title: The Conversion of the Official
events.summary: While returning to the queen’s court, the official is baptized and converted to Christ.
developments: The official is reading Isaiah the prophet in his chariot (Acts 8:28)
Philip explains the gospel of Jesus from the passage in Isaiah 53 (Acts 8:30-35)
The eunuch believes and is baptized in water by the roadside (Acts 8:36-38)
He goes on his way rejoicing toward the queen's kingdom (Acts 8:39)
events.significance: The official became the first recorded African Christian, likely bringing the faith to the queen's palace.

label: Cephas
overview: Cephas is the Aramaic name for the Apostle Peter, meaning 'Rock.' This name was personally given to him by Jesus at their first meeting to signify his future role as a stable foundation for the church. While the name 'Peter' (Greek) is more common in the Gospels, the Apostle Paul frequently uses 'Cephas' in his letters, particularly when discussing the early church's leadership and the conflict in Antioch. Cephas was recognized as one of the three 'pillars' of the Jerusalem church and served as the primary apostle to the Jewish people. His name remains a symbol of the transformation of a vacillating fisherman into a solid and authoritative leader of the global Christian movement.

events.title: The Renaming at the Jordan
events.summary: Jesus gives Simon the new name 'Cephas' during their very first encounter.
developments: Andrew brings his brother Simon to Jesus (John 1:41)
Jesus looks at him and says, 'You shall be called Cephas' (John 1:42)
The text notes that Cephas means Peter (or Rock) (John 1:42)
The naming occurs before Simon had performed any act of leadership (John 1:42)
events.significance: The name was a prophetic designation of the character Jesus would build into him.

events.title: The Rock of the Church
events.summary: Jesus uses the meaning of the name to declare the foundation of His future community.
developments: Simon confesses Jesus as the Christ, the Son of the living God (Matthew 16:16)
Jesus says, 'You are Peter (Rock), and on this rock I will build my church' (Matthew 16:18)
He promises to give him the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 16:19)
The play on words links the name Cephas/Peter to the church's stability (Matthew 16:18)
events.significance: This established the name as a title of apostolic authority and foundational leadership.

events.title: Factions in Corinth
events.summary: The name Cephas is used by a group in Corinth to claim a specific line of religious authority.
developments: The church is divided into various followings (1 Corinthians 1:11)
Some say, 'I follow Paul,' or 'I follow Apollos' (1 Corinthians 1:12)
A specific group says, 'I follow Cephas' (1 Corinthians 1:12)
Paul uses the name to emphasize that all leaders belong to the church, not the other way around (1 Corinthians 3:22)
events.significance: The use of 'Cephas' suggests the influence of Jewish-Christian tradition in Corinth.

events.title: Rights of an Apostle
events.summary: Paul references the marital status and travels of Cephas to defend his own ministry.
developments: Paul asks if he has the right to take along a believing wife (1 Corinthians 9:5)
He notes that the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord do so (1 Corinthians 10:5)
He specifically names Cephas as one who travels with his wife (1 Corinthians 9:5)
This provides a rare glimpse into the domestic life of the lead apostle (1 Corinthians 9:5)
events.significance: Cephas served as the standard for apostolic practice in the early church.

events.title: The First Witness
events.summary: In the official creed of the resurrection, Cephas is listed as the first male apostle to see the risen Lord.
developments: Paul delivers the tradition of Christ's death and burial (1 Corinthians 15:3-4)
He states that Christ appeared to Cephas (1 Corinthians 15:5)
Then he appeared to the Twelve (1 Corinthians 15:5)
This prioritizes the personal restoration of the lead apostle (1 Corinthians 15:5)
events.significance: Cephas’s eyewitness testimony was the cornerstone of the resurrection proclamation.

events.title: Meeting with Paul
events.summary: Paul travels to Jerusalem specifically to visit Cephas three years after his conversion.
developments: Paul goes up to Jerusalem to 'visit Cephas' (Galatians 1:18)
He stays with him for fifteen days (Galatians 1:18)
He sees no other apostle except James (Galatians 1:19)
The visit established a personal link between the Apostle to the Gentiles and the Rock (Galatians 1:18)
events.significance: This meeting highlights the high regard in which Cephas was held by the entire movement.

events.title: The Pillar of Jerusalem
events.summary: Cephas is recognized as one of the three primary leaders of the church in the capital.
developments: Paul returns to Jerusalem after fourteen years (Galatians 2:1)
He meets with those who seemed to be influential (Galatians 2:2)
James, Cephas, and John are identified as 'pillars' (Galatians 2:9)
They give Paul the right hand of fellowship for his mission (Galatians 2:9)
events.significance: Cephas officially validated the mission to the Gentiles while focusing on the Jews.

events.title: Conflict at Antioch
events.summary: Paul publicly rebukes Cephas for withdrawing from table fellowship with Gentiles.
developments: Cephas comes to Antioch and initially eats with the Gentiles (Galatians 2:11-12)
When men from James arrive, he separates himself for fear of the circumcision party (Galatians 2:12)
Paul opposes him to his face because he stood condemned (Galatians 2:11)
Paul calls his behavior hypocrisy and a denial of the gospel's truth (Galatians 2:14)
events.significance: This event showed that even 'The Rock' was capable of significant spiritual error.

events.title: Solomon builds a high place for Chemosh east of Jerusalem

label: Christ
overview: Christ is the Greek-derived title (Christos) for the Hebrew 'Messiah,' meaning 'The Anointed One.' In the biblical narrative, Jesus is identified as the Christ—the long-awaited heir of King David and the suffering servant of the prophets who would redeem Israel and the world. The title signifies that Jesus was uniquely set apart and empowered by the Holy Spirit for the offices of Prophet, Priest, and King. While Jesus often kept His identity as the Christ a secret during His early ministry, His resurrection confirmed His status to the world. The term transitioned from a title to a name, forming the basis of the identity of His followers, who became known as Christians.

events.title: The Promised Anointed One
events.summary: The Old Testament establishes the expectation of a future 'Anointed' King who will rule the nations.
developments: The kings of the earth plot against the Lord and His Anointed (Psalm 2:2)
He is promised the nations as an inheritance (Psalm 2:8)
Daniel speaks of the time when 'Messiah (Anointed One) the Prince' shall come (Daniel 9:25)
Isaiah describes the Spirit of the Lord resting on the branch from Jesse (Isaiah 11:1-2)
events.significance: The title Christ was rooted in centuries of prophetic longing and covenant promise.

events.title: The Proclamation at Birth
events.summary: Angels announce the birth of Jesus using the specific title of Christ.
developments: The angel tells the shepherds, 'Unto you is born... a Savior, who is Christ the Lord' (Luke 2:11)
Simeon is told he will not see death before he sees the 'Lord's Christ' (Luke 2:26)
He identifies the child as the 'light for revelation to the Gentiles' (Luke 2:32)
The title links the infant directly to the throne of David (Luke 2:11)
events.significance: The identity of Jesus as the Christ was settled by divine decree at His birth.

events.title: Anointing by the Spirit
events.summary: Jesus is formally 'anointed' for His work during His baptism and first sermon.
developments: The Spirit of God descends like a dove upon Him (Matthew 3:16)
A voice from heaven declares Him the beloved Son (Matthew 3:17)
In Nazareth, Jesus reads: 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me' (Luke 4:18)
He declares that this prophecy is fulfilled in their hearing (Luke 4:21)
events.significance: His baptism was the public inaugural event of His work as the Christ.

events.title: The Great Confession
events.summary: Peter recognizes and articulates Jesus’ identity as the Christ on behalf of the disciples.
developments: Jesus asks His disciples, 'Who do you say that I am?' (Matthew 16:15)
Peter says, 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God' (Matthew 16:16)
Jesus says this was revealed by His Father in heaven (Matthew 16:17)
He strictly charges them to tell no one yet that He is the Christ (Matthew 16:20)
events.significance: This was the foundational moment for the understanding of the apostolic community.

events.title: Affirmation before the Sanhedrin
events.summary: Under trial for His life, Jesus officially accepts the title in a public, legal setting.
developments: The high priest asks, 'Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?' (Mark 14:61)
Jesus replies, 'I am' (Mark 14:62)
He speaks of the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power (Mark 14:62)
This confession leads to His immediate condemnation for blasphemy (Mark 14:63-64)
events.significance: Jesus chose to confirm His identity when it meant certain death.

events.title: Mockery on the Cross
events.summary: The title of Christ is used as a term of ridicule during the crucifixion.
developments: The rulers scoff, saying, 'Let him save himself, if he is the Christ' (Luke 23:35)
One of the criminals rails at Him: 'Are you not the Christ? Save yourself and us!' (Luke 23:39)
The sign above Him reads 'King of the Jews,' the political equivalent of Christ (Luke 23:38)
He dies as the 'Rejected Christ' in the eyes of the world (Luke 23:33-46)
events.significance: The crucifixion fulfilled the 'Suffering Servant' aspect of the Messianic role.

events.title: Proclamation at Pentecost
events.summary: Peter preaches that the resurrection has proven Jesus is both Lord and Christ.
developments: Peter argues from the Psalms that David spoke of the Christ's resurrection (Acts 2:31)
He declares that God has made Jesus 'both Lord and Christ' (Acts 2:36)
The crowd is 'cut to the heart' and 3,000 are baptized (Acts 2:37-41)
The mission of the church begins with this specific Christological claim (Acts 2:36)
events.significance: The resurrection turned the title into the central message of global salvation.

events.title: The Work of Christ
events.summary: Paul explains the theological implications of what Jesus accomplished as the Anointed One.
developments: While we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly (Romans 5:6)
We are justified by His blood and saved from wrath (Romans 5:9)
There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1)
Nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 8:39)
events.significance: The title became the foundation of Christian doctrine and spiritual life.

events.title: The Returning Christ
events.summary: The biblical narrative concludes with the vision of Christ returning to rule the earth.
developments: The kingdoms of this world become the kingdom of our Lord and His Christ (Revelation 11:15)
He is seen as the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:6-12)
He returns as King of kings and Lord of lords (Revelation 19:16)
He will reign forever and ever (Revelation 11:15)
events.significance: The story of the Christ ends with the total triumph of His eternal Kingdom.

label: Counselor
overview: In the biblical context, 'Counselor' (or Comforter/Advocate) is a specific title used by Jesus to describe the Holy Spirit. During the Last Supper, Jesus promised His disciples that although He was leaving, the Father would send 'another Counselor' to be with them forever. This entity is defined as the Spirit of Truth, tasked with teaching the believers, reminding them of Jesus' words, and bearing witness to Christ in the world. The Counselor serves as the divine presence within the church, providing guidance, conviction of sin, and the power to sustain faith in the face of opposition.

events.title: The Promise of Presence
events.summary: Jesus promises to ask the Father for a Counselor to replace His physical presence.
developments: Jesus says He will pray the Father to give 'another Counselor' (John 14:16)
The Counselor is identified as the 'Spirit of Truth' (John 14:17)
The world cannot receive Him, but the disciples know Him (John 14:17)
He is promised to dwell with the believers and be in them (John 14:17)
events.significance: The title establishes the Holy Spirit as the personal continuation of Jesus' ministry.

events.title: The Divine Teacher
events.summary: The Counselor's role is defined as the primary instructor and memory-enhancer for the church.
developments: Jesus states the Father will send the Counselor in His name (John 14:26)
He will teach the disciples all things (John 14:26)
He will bring to remembrance all that Jesus said to them (John 14:26)
His teaching provides a supernatural peace that the world cannot give (John 14:27)
events.significance: This explains the source of the apostles' deep understanding and the preservation of the Gospels.

events.title: The Witness in Persecution
events.summary: Jesus reveals that the Counselor will empower believers to testify when facing hatred.
developments: Jesus warns that the world will hate the disciples (John 15:18-21)
He says when the Counselor comes, He will bear witness about Jesus (John 15:26)
The Counselor proceeds from the Father (John 15:26)
The disciples are then enabled to bear witness because of His presence (John 15:27)
events.significance: The Counselor is the engine of the church's courage and evangelism.

events.title: The Work of Conviction
events.summary: Jesus explains the Counselor's judicial role in addressing the world's sin and righteousness.
developments: Jesus says it is to the disciples' advantage that He goes away (John 16:7)
If He goes, He will send the Counselor to them (John 16:7)
The Counselor will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment (John 16:8-11)
He will guide the believers into all the truth (John 16:13)
events.significance: The Holy Spirit acts as a legal advocate for God's truth in the court of human conscience.

events.title: The Manifestation and Comfort
events.summary: The early church experiences the literal arrival and ongoing 'comfort' of the Counselor.
developments: The Spirit descends on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:1-4)
Peter proclaims this is the fulfillment of the promise of the Spirit (Acts 2:33)
The church throughout Judea and Galilee has peace and is built up (Acts 9:31)
The text notes the church walked in the 'comfort of the Holy Spirit' (Acts 9:31)
events.significance: The abstract promise of the Counselor became the living reality of the Christian community.

label: Cretans
overview: The Cretans were the inhabitants of the Mediterranean island of Crete, a group mentioned in both the history and the pastoral epistles of the New Testament. They were among the diverse ethnic groups present in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost, witnessing the first outpouring of the Holy Spirit. Later, the Apostle Paul visited the island and left Titus there to organize the fledgling local churches. Paul famously quoted one of their own poets to describe the cultural challenges in Crete, characterizing the people as 'always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.' Despite this harsh cultural assessment, the Cretans represent a community where the gospel was effectively planted and where believers were urged to model good works to transform their reputation.

events.title: Witnesses at Pentecost
events.summary: Jews from Crete are present in Jerusalem to witness the birth of the church.
developments: The Holy Spirit falls on the 120 in the upper room (Acts 2:1-4)
Cretans and Arabians are explicitly named among the crowd (Acts 2:11)
They hear the apostles telling the mighty works of God in their own tongues (Acts 2:11)
This indicates that the seeds of the gospel likely returned to the island very early (Acts 2:1-11)
events.significance: The Cretans were part of the original international audience for the first Christian sermon.

events.title: The Stormy Voyage
events.summary: Paul visits the island of Crete during his perilous journey as a prisoner to Rome.
developments: The ship sails under the lee of Crete off Salmone (Acts 27:7)
They arrive at a place called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea (Acts 27:8)
Paul warns the centurion that sailing further will be disastrous (Acts 27:10)
They attempt to reach Phoenix, a harbor of Crete, but are caught in a tempest (Acts 27:12-15)
events.significance: The geography of Crete played a central role in the drama of Paul's survival.

events.title: Church Planting and Order
events.summary: Paul leaves Titus in Crete to complete the organization of the local Christian communities.
developments: Paul explains he left Titus in Crete to put things in order (Titus 1:5)
Titus is commanded to appoint elders in every town (Titus 1:5)
Paul warns of 'insubordinate' people on the island, especially of the circumcision party (Titus 1:10)
He notes that teachers are upsetting whole families for shameful gain (Titus 1:11)
events.significance: Crete was a challenging mission field that required strong, character-driven leadership.

events.title: The Cultural Reputation
events.summary: Paul quotes a Cretan prophet to emphasize the moral difficulty of the island's culture.
developments: A prophet of their own said, 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons' (Titus 1:12)
Paul affirms that 'this testimony is true' (Titus 1:13)
He commands Titus to rebuke them sharply so they may be sound in faith (Titus 1:13)
The goal was to overcome a culture of deceit with the truth of the gospel (Titus 1:14-16)
events.significance: The passage provides a rare, direct look at the ethnographic challenges of first-century missions.

events.title: The Call to Good Works
events.summary: Paul urges the Cretan believers to live lives that contradict their national reputation.
developments: Believers are to be models of good works (Titus 2:7)
Slaves are to be submissive to show the beauty of the doctrine of God (Titus 2:9-10)
They are to be ready for every good work and to speak evil of no one (Titus 3:1-2)
Paul emphasizes that the Cretan church should excel in 'honest trades' to meet urgent needs (Titus 3:14)
events.significance: The Cretans were called to be a distinct counter-culture within their own society.

label: Demetrius
overview: Demetrius was a silversmith in the city of Ephesus who specialized in making silver shrines of the goddess Artemis. He is most famous for inciting a massive riot against the Apostle Paul, whose preaching was causing many people to abandon idolatry, thereby threatening Demetrius’s lucrative business. By appealing to both the economic fears and the religious pride of the craftsmen, he triggered an uproar that filled the city’s massive theater for two hours. In another context, the name Demetrius refers to a faithful Christian mentioned by John as a man of good report from everyone and from the truth itself, representing the total contrast between an enemy and a friend of the gospel.

label: Edom
overview: Edom was the nation descended from Esau, the twin brother of Jacob, located in the rugged mountainous region south of the Dead Sea. The relationship between Edom and Israel was characterized by a long-standing and bitter rivalry that began in the womb and persisted through the centuries. Edom famously refused Israel passage during the Exodus and later rejoiced over the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians. The prophets frequently condemned Edom for their pride and their 'everlasting enmity' toward their brother nation. Edom serves as a biblical symbol of the worldly and arrogant spirit that opposes the purposes of God.

events.title: Ancestral Origins
events.summary: The nation of Edom begins with Esau, who sells his birthright for a bowl of red stew.
developments: Esau is given the name Edom, meaning 'Red' (Genesis 25:30)
He settles in the hill country of Seir (Genesis 36:8)
Esau is explicitly called 'the father of the Edomites' (Genesis 36:9)
The genealogy lists the chiefs and kings who reigned before any king in Israel (Genesis 36:31)
events.significance: Edom’s identity was forged in the rejection of spiritual heritage for physical appetite.

events.title: Refusal of Passage
events.summary: During the wilderness wandering, the King of Edom denies Israel permission to cross his land.
developments: Moses sends messengers appealing to their shared brotherhood (Numbers 20:14)
Edom refuses and threatens Israel with the sword (Numbers 20:18)
He comes out with a large army and a strong hand (Numbers 20:20)
Israel is forced to turn away and take a longer route (Numbers 20:21)
events.significance: This act of hostility set the tone for all future interactions between the two nations.

events.title: Conquest by the Monarchy
events.summary: Saul and David bring Edom under Israelite military control.
developments: Saul fights against Edom and inflicts punishment (1 Samuel 14:47)
David defeats 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt (2 Samuel 8:13)
David puts garrisons throughout all Edom (2 Samuel 8:14)
The Edomites become servants/vassals to King David (2 Samuel 8:14)
events.significance: This fulfilled the prophecy that the older (Esau/Edom) would serve the younger (Jacob/Israel).

events.title: The Adversary Hadad
events.summary: A survivor of David’s purge, Hadad the Edomite, rises as a persistent rival to Solomon.
developments: Hadad flees to Egypt as a child during Joab's campaign (1 Kings 11:17)
He finds favor with Pharaoh and marries into the Egyptian royal family (1 Kings 11:19)
Upon David’s death, Hadad returns to trouble Israel (1 Kings 11:21-22)
God raises him up as an 'adversary' to Solomon in his later years (1 Kings 11:14)
events.significance: Edomite resistance served as a divine discipline for Solomon’s idolatry.

events.title: Revolt and Independence
events.summary: Edom successfully breaks free from Judean control during the reign of King Jehoram.
developments: Edom revolts against the rule of Judah and sets up its own king (2 Kings 8:20)
Jehoram attempts to crush the revolt at Zair but fails to retake the land (2 Kings 8:21)
The text notes that Edom remained in revolt 'to this day' (2 Kings 8:22)
The loss of Edom signaled the declining power of the southern kingdom (2 Chronicles 21:8-10)
events.significance: The permanent break from Judah marked the end of the Davidic empire's southern reach.

events.title: The Betrayal of Jerusalem
events.summary: Edom assists the Babylonians in the destruction of Jerusalem, earning severe prophetic judgment.
developments: Edomites cried 'Raze it! Raze it!' as Jerusalem fell (Psalm 137:7)
They stood aloof and rejoiced over the day of their brother's ruin (Obadiah 1:11-12)
They entered the gates of the city to loot and cut off fugitives (Obadiah 1:13-14)
Obadiah prophesies the total destruction of the house of Esau (Obadiah 1:18)
events.significance: Edom’s lack of brotherly compassion became the focus of intense divine wrath.

events.title: Prophecy of Perpetual Desolation
events.summary: Ezekiel pronounces a doom on Mount Seir (Edom) for its 'everlasting enmity'.
developments: God sets His face against Mount Seir to make it a desolation (Ezekiel 35:3)
The cause is identified as Edom's desire to seize the two nations of Israel and Judah (Ezekiel 35:10)
God promises to prepare them for blood because they did not hate bloodshed (Ezekiel 35:6)
The desolation is meant to prove that 'I am the Lord' (Ezekiel 35:15)
events.significance: Edom became the representative of all who attempt to profit from the suffering of God's people.

events.title: The Final Verdict
events.summary: The Old Testament closes with a declaration of God’s love for Jacob and hatred for Esau (Edom).
developments: The Lord says, 'I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated' (Malachi 1:2-3)
Edom's mountains are made a waste and his heritage given to jackals (Malachi 1:3)
Edom vows to rebuild the ruins, but God says He will tear them down (Malachi 1:4)
They are called the 'territory of wickedness' (Malachi 1:4)
events.significance: The end of the Edomite story serves as a lesson in the permanence of divine election.

label: Egyptians
overview: The Egyptians were the dominant superpower of the ancient Near East and played a central, recurring role in the biblical story. Initially a place of refuge for the patriarchs, Egypt became a site of brutal bondage for the Israelites, leading to the climactic Exodus and the definitive revelation of God’s power over pagan deities. Throughout the Monarchy, Egypt was often a tempting but unreliable political ally for Israel and Judah, frequently drawing the rebuke of the prophets. Historically and symbolically, the Egyptians represent the 'house of slavery' from which God delivers His people, yet they are also included in future promises of global redemption.

events.title: Place of Refuge and Rise
events.summary: Egypt serves as a sanctuary for Abraham during famine and later becomes the site of Joseph’s exaltation.
developments: Abraham goes down to Egypt to stay because of a severe famine (Genesis 12:10)

Joseph rises to become second-in-command over all Egypt (Genesis 41:41)

events.title: The Era of Bondage

events.significance: This oppression created the cry for help that triggered the Exodus.

events.title: The Ten Plagues
events.summary: God executes judgments against the Egyptians and their gods to force the release of Israel.
developments: The Nile is turned to blood, affecting the Egyptians' primary water source (Exodus 7:20-21)
The Egyptians suffer through infestations of frogs, gnats, and flies (Exodus 8)
Darkness covers the land of Egypt while Israel has light (Exodus 10:22-23)
The death of the firstborn strikes every Egyptian house (Exodus 12:29-30)
events.significance: The plagues demonstrated the supremacy of Yahweh over the Egyptian pantheon.

events.title: The Red Sea Disaster
events.summary: The Egyptian army pursues Israel and is destroyed in the return of the waters.
developments: Pharaoh leads 600 chosen chariots in pursuit (Exodus 14:6-7)
The Egyptians march into the middle of the sea on dry ground (Exodus 14:23)
The Lord clogs their chariot wheels and throws them into a panic (Exodus 14:24-25)
The entire army is covered by the sea, and not one remains (Exodus 14:28)
events.significance: The event was the final, physical break from Egyptian power.

events.title: The Solomonic Alliance
events.summary: Solomon enters into a diplomatic and marital alliance with the Egyptians.
developments: Solomon marries the daughter of Pharaoh (1 Kings 3:1)
Pharaoh captures Gezer and gives it as a dowry for his daughter (1 Kings 9:16)
Egypt becomes a primary source for Solomon's horses and chariots (1 Kings 10:28)
Egyptian influence contributes to the spiritual compromise of the king (1 Kings 11:1-4)
events.significance: The alliance marked a dangerous return to reliance on the 'broken reed' of Egypt.

events.title: The Invasion of Shishak
events.summary: The Egyptians invade Judah and plunder the Temple gold during the reign of Rehoboam.
developments: Shishak, king of Egypt, comes up against Jerusalem (1 Kings 14:25)
He has 1,200 chariots and 60,000 horsemen (2 Chronicles 12:3)
He takes away the treasures of the house of the Lord (1 Kings 14:26)
He carries off the 500 gold shields Solomon had made (1 Kings 14:26)
events.significance: This invasion stripped Judah of its imperial wealth and reduced its regional status.

events.title: The Death of Josiah

developments: Pharaoh Neco goes up to the River Euphrates to help the king of Assyria (2 Kings 23:29)
Josiah goes out to meet him in battle (2 Kings 23:29)
Neco kills Josiah at Megiddo as soon as he sees him (2 Kings 23:29)
Judah becomes an Egyptian vassal for a short time following the battle (2 Kings 23:33-35)
events.significance: Egyptian intervention accelerated the final collapse of the Kingdom of Judah.

events.title: Future Conversion
events.summary: The prophets predict a day when Egypt will abandon idols and worship the true God.
developments: The Lord will make Himself known to the Egyptians (Isaiah 19:21)
Egyptians will worship with sacrifice and offerings (Isaiah 19:21)

label: Foreigners
overview: Foreigners, often referred to as 'sojourners' or 'aliens,' hold a unique and protected status within the biblical narrative. In the Old Testament, the Law of Moses commanded Israel to show kindness and justice to foreigners, reminding the people that they too were once foreigners in Egypt. While excluded from certain ritual activities, foreigners who worshipped God were often included in the blessings of the community, as seen in the stories of Rahab and Ruth. In the New Testament, the concept expanded as the gospel broke down ethnic barriers, declaring that in Christ there is no longer 'foreigner or stranger,' but all are fellow citizens of the kingdom of God.

events.significance: This established Israel as a welcoming community based on faith rather than just blood.

events.title: Sacrificial Equality
