Provision is made for corporate atonement including the foreigner (Numbers 15:26)
events.significance: Foreigners were spiritually integrated into the sacrificial system.

events.title: The Right to Glean
events.summary: The Law ensures that foreigners have access to food through the practice of gleaning.
developments: Farmers are commanded not to reap to the very edges of their fields (Leviticus 19:9-10)
The leftovers are for the poor and the sojourner (Leviticus 23:22)
Ruth the Moabite utilizes this right in the fields of Boaz (Ruth 2:2)
Boaz shows 'hesed' (kindness) to the foreigner beyond the legal minimum (Ruth 2:8-16)
events.significance: The social safety net of Israel specifically included non-Israelites.

events.title: Solomon’s Temple Prayer

The goal is that all peoples of the earth may know God's name (1 Kings 8:43)
The Temple is intended to be a 'house of prayer for all peoples' (Isaiah 56:7)
events.significance: The Temple was established with a global, missional vision.

events.title: The End of Alienation

Announces John's birth to Zechariah and declares that he will be unable to speak
Tells Mary she will bear Jesus, the Son of God

label: Gad
overview: Son of Jacob and Zilpah, named by Leah when she called his birth fortunate. Jacob's blessing said raiders would attack Gad, but he would attack their heels.

details.label: Family
details.value: Son of Jacob and Zilpah; brother of Asher

label: Gaius
overview: Gaius was a common Roman name held by several early Christians associated with the Apostle Paul and his mission. One Gaius was a Macedonian traveling companion of Paul who was seized by the mob during the riot in Ephesus. Another was a resident of Derbe who accompanied Paul on his final journey to Jerusalem. Most significantly, Paul mentions a Gaius in Corinth whom he personally baptized and who served as a host to both the apostle and the entire local church. Additionally, the Apostle John addressed his third epistle to a 'beloved Gaius,' praising him for his hospitality and faithfulness to the truth. These figures exemplify the hospitality and loyalty that sustained the early global church.

events.title: Victim of the Ephesus Riot
events.summary: A Macedonian named Gaius is caught in the violent uproar in Ephesus.
developments: The city is filled with confusion (Acts 19:29)
The mob seizes Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul's companions (Acts 19:29)
They are dragged into the massive theater (Acts 19:29)
They are eventually released after the town clerk quietens the crowd (Acts 19:35-41)
events.significance: Gaius personally suffered for his association with Paul's ministry.

events.title: Traveling to Jerusalem
events.summary: A different Gaius, from the city of Derbe, joins Paul’s international delegation.
developments: Paul decides to return through Macedonia to Jerusalem (Acts 20:3)
Gaius of Derbe is listed among the companions (Acts 20:4)
The group includes representatives from various Gentile churches (Acts 20:4)
They go ahead to Troas to wait for Paul (Acts 20:5)
events.significance: He represented the Galatian churches in delivering the collection for Judea.

events.title: Baptized by Paul
events.summary: Paul notes that he personally performed the baptism of a man named Gaius in Corinth.
developments: Paul writes to address factions in the Corinthian church (1 Corinthians 1:11-13)
He thanks God that he baptized only a few individuals (1 Corinthians 1:14)
He specifically names Gaius as one of the exceptions (1 Corinthians 1:14)
This indicates Gaius was a foundational member of the Corinthian assembly (1 Corinthians 1:14-17)
events.significance: The personal involvement of Paul highlights Gaius's importance in Corinth.

events.title: Host of the Whole Church
events.summary: While Paul is in Corinth, he identifies Gaius as a remarkably hospitable man.
developments: Paul writes the letter to the Romans from Corinth (Romans 16:1)
He sends greetings from 'Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church' (Romans 16:23)
This suggests Gaius's home was the primary meeting place for the Christians (Romans 16:23)
His wealth and generosity provided a base for the apostle's labor (Romans 16:23)
events.significance: Gaius was the domestic and logistical anchor for the church in a major city.

events.title: Recipient of John's Letter
events.summary: The Apostle John writes a personal letter to a faithful leader named Gaius.
developments: John addresses him as 'the beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth' (3 John 1:1)
He prays for Gaius’s health and prosperity (3 John 1:2)
He commends Gaius for walking in the truth and showing hospitality to strangers (3 John 1:3-6)
He contrasts Gaius's faithfulness with the arrogance of Diotrephes (3 John 1:9-12)
events.significance: This Gaius represents the ideal local leader who supports the global mission.

label: Gallio
overview: Proconsul of Achaia who refused to judge the complaint against Paul, calling it a dispute about Jewish law. He drove the accusers away and showed no concern when the crowd beat Sosthenes.

label: Gamaliel
overview: Pharisee and teacher of the law respected by the people. He urged the Sanhedrin to leave the apostles alone, warning that it could be opposing God. Paul later named him as his teacher in Jerusalem.

details.label: Role
details.value: Pharisee and teacher of the law in the Sanhedrin

label: Gedaliah
overview: Appointed by Babylon's king to govern the people left in Judah. He urged them to remain and serve Babylon, but dismissed Johanan's warning of a murder plot. Ishmael son of Nethaniah killed him at Mizpah.

card.role: Governor of Judah after Jerusalem's fall

details.label: Role
details.value: Governor over those left in Judah

details.label: Family
details.value: Son of Ahikam and grandson of Shaphan

events.title: Governs at Mizpah and urges the returning people to serve Babylon
Dismisses Johanan's warning that Ishmael plans to kill him
Is murdered by Ishmael and his men at Mizpah

label: Gehazi
overview: Served the prophet Elisha. He lied to obtain silver and clothing from Naaman after Elisha had accepted no gift, then lied to Elisha about where he had been. Elisha pronounced judgment, and Gehazi left with leprosy.

events.title: Tells Elisha that the Shunammite woman has no son
Lays Elisha's staff on the dead boy, but the boy does not respond
Lies to Naaman to obtain silver and clothing, then hides them
Lies to Elisha and receives the judgment of Naaman's leprosy
Tells the king about Elisha and identifies the woman whose son was restored

label: Gentiles
overview: Gentiles refers to all nations and peoples outside of the ethnic and covenantal lineage of Israel. Throughout the Old Testament, the relationship between Israel and the Gentiles was one of separation punctuated by occasional inclusion, as God intended Israel to be a 'light to the nations.' The prophets frequently spoke of a future day when the Gentiles would come to Jerusalem to worship the true God. This culminated in the New Testament with the Great Commission, where the gospel was officially extended to all ethnicities. The inclusion of the Gentiles into the church was the central theological drama of the early apostles, establishing the global and multi-ethnic nature of the family of God.

events.title: The Promise to the Nations
events.summary: God establishes from the beginning that the blessing given to Abraham is for all Gentiles.
developments: God promises Abraham that in him all the families of the earth shall be blessed (Genesis 12:3)
He reiterates that in Abraham's offspring all the nations (Gentiles) shall be blessed (Genesis 22:18)
The focus of the covenant is outward-facing toward the world (Genesis 18:18)
Israel is chosen to be the vehicle of this global favor (Genesis 12:1-3)
events.significance: This established the theological purpose of Israel as a missionary people.

events.title: Legal Status of Sojourners
events.summary: The Mosaic Law provided specific protections and a path for Gentiles to live within Israel.
developments: Israel is forbidden from oppressing the sojourner/foreigner (Exodus 22:21)
Provision is made for Gentiles to offer sacrifices (Numbers 15:14-16)
Circumcised Gentiles are permitted to eat the Passover (Exodus 12:48)
One law was to apply to both the native and the Gentile among them (Numbers 15:15)
events.significance: The Law prevented ethnic exclusion based on mere ancestry.

events.title: The Light to the Nations
events.summary: Prophetic literature identifies the coming Messiah as the light for the Gentiles.
developments: The Servant is appointed as a covenant for the people and a light for the nations (Isaiah 42:6)
God says it is 'too light a thing' to restore only Israel (Isaiah 49:6)
The salvation of God is intended to reach to the end of the earth (Isaiah 49:6)
Nations are depicted as coming to Zion to learn the ways of God (Isaiah 2:2-4)
events.significance: The prophets expanded the scope of salvation from national to global.

events.title: The First Gentile Worshippers
events.summary: The birth of Jesus is immediately recognized by Gentile scholars from the East.
developments: Magi from the east arrive in Jerusalem seeking the King of the Jews (Matthew 2:1-2)
They follow a star that leads them to Bethlehem (Matthew 2:9)
They fall down and worship the infant Jesus (Matthew 2:11)
They present gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh (Matthew 2:11)
events.significance: This event signaled that the Messiah’s arrival had immediate significance for the Gentile world.

events.title: The Opening of the Kingdom
events.summary: Jesus interacts with Gentile faith and ultimately commissions a global mission.
developments: Jesus praises the 'great faith' of the Canaanite woman (Matthew 15:21-28)
He heals the servant of a Roman centurion (Matthew 8:5-13)
Jesus gives the Great Commission to 'make disciples of all nations' (Matthew 28:19)
The Gospel is to be preached as a testimony to all the Gentiles (Matthew 24:14)
events.significance: Jesus removed the priority of the 'lost sheep of Israel' in favor of the whole world.

events.title: The Inclusion of Cornelius
events.summary: The Apostle Peter is divinely directed to baptize the first uncircumcised Gentiles.
developments: Peter sees a vision of clean and unclean animals (Acts 10:9-16)
He goes to the house of the Roman centurion Cornelius (Acts 10:24-25)
The Holy Spirit falls on the Gentiles while Peter is preaching (Acts 10:44)
Peter realizes 'God shows no partiality' between Jew and Gentile (Acts 10:34-35)
events.significance: This was the watershed moment that settled the issue of Gentile membership in the church.

events.title: The Council of Jerusalem
events.summary: The church leaders formally decide that Gentiles do not need to follow the Mosaic Law.
developments: A conflict arises over whether Gentiles must be circumcised (Acts 15:1-5)
Peter, Paul, and Barnabas testify to God’s work among the nations (Acts 15:7-12)
James delivers the verdict that no unnecessary burden be placed on Gentiles (Acts 15:19)
The gospel of the uncircumcision is committed to Paul (Galatians 2:7)
events.significance: The decision established the theological freedom and equality of Gentile believers.

events.title: The Mystery Revealed
events.summary: Paul explains the theological unity of Jews and Gentiles in the body of Christ.
developments: The 'dividing wall of hostility' has been broken down (Ephesians 2:14)
Gentiles are now 'fellow heirs' and 'members of the same body' (Ephesians 3:6)
They are no longer strangers and aliens but fellow citizens (Ephesians 2:19)
The union of both groups into one new man was a hidden mystery now revealed (Ephesians 3:3-5)
events.significance: The Gentile story ends with total spiritual integration into the people of God.

label: Gerasenes
overview: The Gerasenes were the inhabitants of a specific region on the eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee, primarily known as a site of Jesus' power over the demonic realm. In their territory, Jesus encountered a man possessed by a 'Legion' of demons who lived among the tombs and was untamable by human means. After Jesus cast the demons into a herd of pigs, which then drowned in the sea, the Gerasenes were overcome with fear and pleaded with Jesus to leave their region. While the people rejected His presence due to economic loss and terror, the healed man became the first evangelist to the Decapolis, testifying to the mercy Jesus had shown him.

events.title: Arrival in the Region
events.summary: Jesus and His disciples cross the sea to the country of the Gerasenes.
developments: They come to the other side of the sea (Mark 5:1)
The region is also referred to as the land of the Gadarenes or Gergesenes (Matthew 8:28 / Luke 8:26)
It was a predominantly Gentile area on the eastern shore (Mark 5:11)
As soon as Jesus steps out of the boat, He is met by a demon-possessed man (Mark 5:2)
events.significance: This was one of Jesus' few recorded missions into primarily non-Jewish territory.

events.title: The Legion and the Swine
events.summary: Jesus heals the possessed man and the demons enter a massive herd of local livestock.
developments: The demons identify themselves as 'Legion' (Mark 5:9)
They beg not to be sent out of the country (Mark 5:10)
Jesus permits them to enter a herd of about 2,000 pigs (Mark 5:11-13)
The herd rushes down the steep bank and drowns in the sea (Mark 5:13)
events.significance: The event demonstrated Christ's absolute authority over both the spiritual and physical realms.

events.title: Reaction of the Inhabitants
events.summary: The Gerasenes witness the healed man but prioritize their economic interests over Jesus.
developments: The herdsmen flee and report the event in the city and country (Mark 5:14)
The people see the demoniac sitting there, clothed and in his right mind (Mark 5:15)
They are afraid of the power they have witnessed (Mark 5:15)
They begin to beg Jesus to depart from their region (Mark 5:17)
events.significance: The Gerasenes represent those who are more comfortable with the demonic than with the presence of God.

events.title: Mission to the Decapolis
events.summary: Though the Gerasenes reject Jesus, He leaves them a witness from among their own people.
developments: The healed man begs to go with Jesus (Mark 5:18)
Jesus refuses, telling him to go home and tell how much the Lord has done (Mark 5:19)
The man goes and proclaims the news throughout the Decapolis (Mark 5:20)
All who hear him are amazed at his testimony (Mark 5:20)
events.significance: The Gerasenes were the recipients of the first intentional apostolic mission to the Gentiles.

label: Gideon
overview: Delivered Israel from Midian with three hundred men as the LORD directed. He tore down Baal's altar and refused to rule over Israel. He also killed the men of Penuel and made an ephod that Israel worshiped, ensnaring him and his household.

details.label: Role
details.value: Sent to save Israel from Midian

details.label: Buried
details.value: His father Joash's tomb in Ophrah

events.title: The LORD sends him to save Israel from Midian
Tears down his father's Baal altar and receives the name Jerubbaal
Asks for two signs with a fleece, and God grants them
The LORD chooses three hundred men to deliver Midian into his hand
Attacks with horns and torches as the LORD turns Midian's swords against one another
Punishes Succoth's men and kills Penuel's men
Refuses rule but makes an ephod that Israel worships
Dies in old age and is buried in his father's tomb

label: God
overview: God is the central and supreme Being of the biblical narrative, identified as the eternal Creator, Sustainer, and Redeemer of all that exists. In the Old Testament, He reveals Himself as Yahweh—the covenant-keeping God of Israel who is holy, just, and merciful. The Scriptures portray God as initiating a relationship with humanity, moving through history to restore the fellowship broken at the Fall. In the New Testament, the revelation of God reaches its climax in the person of Jesus Christ, who is described as the 'image of the invisible God.' The story of Scripture is ultimately the account of God's sovereign plan to reconcile all things to Himself for His own glory.

events.title: Creator of the Universe
events.summary: God brings all things into existence by His word and establishes the order of creation.
developments: In the beginning, God creates the heavens and the earth (Genesis 1:1)
He creates humanity in His own image, male and female (Genesis 1:26-27)
God pronounces the creation 'very good' (Genesis 1:31)
He rests on the seventh day, hallowing the rhythm of time (Genesis 2:1-3)
events.significance: This establishes God's absolute ownership and authority over all life.

events.title: Self-Revelation as Yahweh
events.summary: God reveals His personal name and His character to Moses at the burning bush.
developments: He identifies Himself as 'I AM WHO I AM' (Exodus 3:14)
He declares He is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Exodus 3:15)
God proclaims His name as 'merciful and gracious, slow to anger' (Exodus 34:6)
He emphasizes that He will by no means clear the guilty (Exodus 34:7)
events.significance: The name Yahweh signifies God's eternal presence and His commitment to the covenant.

events.title: Giver of the Law
events.summary: God establishes the ethical and ritual standards for His people on Mount Sinai.
developments: He delivers the Ten Commandments to Israel (Exodus 20:1-17)
He commands the people, 'You shall be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy' (Leviticus 19:2)
The Law defines the way humans are to love God and neighbor (Exodus 20 / Deuteronomy 6)
God enters into a formal covenant relationship with the nation (Exodus 24:7-8)
events.significance: The Law revealed God's moral nature and the requirements for dwelling in His presence.

events.title: Establishing the Eternal Kingdom
events.summary: God makes a covenant with David, promising an everlasting throne to his offspring.
developments: God promises to build David a 'house' or dynasty (2 Samuel 7:11)
He declares He will be a father to David's son (2 Samuel 7:14)
The Lord promises that His steadfast love will not depart from him (2 Samuel 7:15)
The throne is established forever as a divine decree (2 Samuel 7:16)
events.significance: This provided the historical and theological foundation for the Messianic hope.

events.title: The Incarnation
events.summary: God becomes flesh in the person of Jesus Christ to dwell among humanity.
developments: The Word was with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1)
The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14)
God so loved the world that He gave His only Son (John 3:16)
Jesus is declared to be the only begotten God who makes the Father known (John 1:18)
events.significance: Jesus Christ is the definitive and final self-revelation of God.

events.title: Outpouring of the Spirit
events.summary: God descends to dwell within His people through the gift of the Holy Spirit.
developments: The Spirit is poured out on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:1-4)
The Spirit is identified as the 'Promise of the Father' (Acts 1:4-5)
God now dwells in the hearts of believers rather than a physical temple (1 Corinthians 3:16)
The Spirit empowers the global mission of the church (Acts 1:8)
events.significance: This marked the transition from external ritual to internal spiritual transformation.

events.title: Final Dwelling with Man
events.summary: The biblical story concludes with God making His permanent home with redeemed humanity.
developments: A new heaven and a new earth are established (Revelation 21:1)
God's dwelling place is now with man (Revelation 21:3)
He will wipe away every tear and death will be no more (Revelation 21:4)
The redeemed will see His face and His name will be on their foreheads (Revelation 22:4)
events.significance: The story of God reaches its goal in the perfect restoration of fellowship and glory.

label: Gog
overview: Ruler from Magog named in Ezekiel's prophecy. God said Gog would lead nations against Israel to plunder it, face His wrath, and fall with his armies on Israel's mountains.

details.label: Role
details.value: Chief prince of Meshech and Tubal

details.label: Buried
details.value: A burial in the Valley of Hamon-gog is foretold

card.note: 'Gog and Magog' names the nations Satan gathers in Revelation 20:7-9. The Bible doesn't say that Ezekiel's Gog is an individual among them.

events.title: God declares Himself against Gog and foretells bringing out his armies
God foretells Gog's evil plan to plunder a people living securely
God announces judgment and Gog's fall on Israel's mountains
God foretells seven years of burning weapons and seven months of burials

label: Goliath
overview: Philistine champion from Gath who challenged Israel for forty days. He mocked David, but David struck him with a sling stone and cut off his head with his own sword.

events.title: Challenges Israel to send a man to fight him
Mocks David and is killed as David faces him in the LORD's name

label: Gomer
overview: Married Hosea after the LORD told him to take a prostitute as his wife to portray Israel's unfaithfulness. Gomer bore three children with names announcing judgment. The LORD told Hosea to love his adulterous wife again, and he bought her.

details.label: Family
details.value: Daughter of Diblaim; mother of Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi

events.title: Marries Hosea and bears Jezreel after the LORD's command
Bears Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi, whose names announce judgment
Hosea buys his wife for silver and barley and requires faithfulness

label: Greeks
overview: The Greeks, often referred to in the New Testament as 'Hellenes,' played a crucial role in the expansion of the early church. While they initially appear as seekers who approached the disciples to see Jesus, they soon became the primary mission field for the Apostle Paul. The Greek language served as the common tongue of the Mediterranean world, allowing the Gospel to cross ethnic and geographic boundaries. In the Book of Acts, the arrival of the Gospel in Greek cities like Athens and Corinth created a collision between biblical truth and Greek philosophy. Paul’s ministry was defined by his effort to unite Jews and Greeks into a single body, declaring that in Christ there is no distinction between the two.

events.title: Seekers at the Feast
events.summary: A group of Greeks approaches the disciples during the Passover, signaling the transition of Jesus' mission to the nations.
developments: Greeks among those who went up to worship ask to see Jesus (John 12:20)
They approach Philip, who then consults with Andrew (John 12:21-22)
Jesus declares, 'The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified' (John 12:23)
Their arrival triggers the teaching on the grain of wheat (John 12:24)
events.significance: The Greeks' inquiry represents the world beginning to seek the Jewish Messiah.

events.title: The Hellenist Dispute
events.summary: Tension arises in the early Jerusalem church between Hebrew-speaking and Greek-speaking Jews.
developments: The Hellenists grumble against the Hebrews (Acts 6:1)
Greek-speaking widows were being neglected in the daily distribution (Acts 6:1)
The apostles appoint seven men with Greek names to handle the crisis (Acts 6:3-5)
This led to the ministry of Stephen and Philip (Acts 6:8, 8:5)
events.significance: This conflict led to the first formal administrative structure in the church.

events.title: Preaching in Antioch
events.summary: Believers begin to preach directly to Greeks in Antioch, leading to a massive turning to the Lord.
developments: Men of Cyprus and Cyrene come to Antioch (Acts 11:20)
They speak to the Hellenists (Greeks), preaching the Lord Jesus (Acts 11:20)
A great number of Greeks believe and turn to God (Acts 11:21)
Barnabas is sent from Jerusalem to oversee the new work (Acts 11:22)
events.significance: Antioch became the first major multi-ethnic center for Christianity.

events.title: Collision with Paganism
events.summary: In Lystra, the Greek-speaking populace attempts to worship Paul and Barnabas as Zeus and Hermes.
developments: Paul heals a man lame from birth (Acts 14:8-10)
The crowds shout in the Lycaonian language (Acts 14:11)
They call Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes (Acts 14:12)
The apostles tear their clothes to stop the sacrifice (Acts 14:14)
events.significance: This encounter highlighted the radical difference between Greek mythology and the Gospel.

events.title: The Areopagus Address
events.summary: Paul engages the philosophers of Athens, using their own culture to point to the Creator.
developments: Epicurean and Stoic philosophers debate Paul (Acts 17:18)
He is brought to the Areopagus to explain his teaching (Acts 17:19)
Paul quotes Greek poets to illustrate God's presence (Acts 17:28)
He calls for repentance in light of the resurrection (Acts 17:30-31)
events.significance: Paul established a model for contextualizing the Gospel for an intellectual Greek audience.

events.title: Establishment in Corinth
events.summary: The Gospel takes deep root in one of the most prominent and decadent cities in Greece.
developments: Paul stays with Aquila and Priscilla in Corinth (Acts 18:1-3)
Many of the Corinthians hear, believe, and are baptized (Acts 18:8)
Gallio, the proconsul, refuses to involve Roman law in religious disputes (Acts 18:14-16)
Paul remains for a year and six months teaching the word (Acts 18:11)
events.significance: The Corinthian church became a primary example of a diverse, Gentile-led congregation.

events.title: The End of Distinction
events.summary: Paul’s theology formalizes the spiritual equality of Jews and Greeks in the New Covenant.
developments: Paul declares the Gospel is power for salvation 'to the Jew first and also to the Greek' (Romans 1:16)
He states there is 'neither Jew nor Greek' in Christ Jesus (Galatians 3:28)
God is identified as the God of both Jews and Gentiles (Romans 3:29)
The 'mystery' of the Gospel is the inclusion of the nations (Ephesians 3:6)
events.significance: This doctrinal shift created the framework for a global, non-ethnic church.

events.title: Wisdom vs. the Cross
events.summary: Paul contrasts the Greek desire for intellectual wisdom with the 'folly' of the cross.
developments: Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:22)
The preaching of Christ crucified is a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles (1 Corinthians 1:23)
Paul argues that the foolishness of God is wiser than men (1 Corinthians 1:25)
Believers are called to find true wisdom in Christ alone (1 Corinthians 1:30)
events.significance: This defined the intellectual boundary between the Gospel and secular humanism.

label: Habakkuk
overview: Questioned God about violence and the use of the Chaldeans for judgment. He received God's answer that the righteous would live by faith, and ended his prayer rejoicing in God even if crops and livestock failed.

card.role: Prophet who questioned God about injustice

events.title: Cries out against violence and hears that God is raising the Chaldeans
Questions God's judgment and hears that the righteous will live by faith
Waits for distress and declares joy in God despite failed crops and livestock

label: Hadad
overview: Hadad was the primary storm and fertility god of the Arameans and Canaanites, whose name also became a frequent title for various kings. In the biblical narrative, 'Hadad the Edomite' is the most prominent human figure with this name, serving as a divinely raised adversary against King Solomon. After escaping Joab’s slaughter in Edom as a child and finding refuge in Egypt, Hadad returned to trouble Israel’s borders during Solomon’s spiritual decline. The name represents both the pagan religious environment of Israel’s neighbors and the political consequences of a king turning away from the Lord.

events.title: The Early Kings of Edom
events.summary: The name Hadad appears early in the genealogies of Edom, representing a line of kings.
developments: Hadad the son of Bedad is listed as the king who defeated Midian (Genesis 36:35)
He reigned in the city of Avith (Genesis 36:35)
Another Hadad is listed as the last king in the pre-monarchy list (1 Chronicles 1:50)
His city was Pau, and his wife was Mehetabel (Genesis 36:39)
events.significance: The name was deeply rooted in the royal identity of the Edomite nation.

events.title: Escape from Joab
events.summary: As a young child of the royal house, Hadad survives David's conquest of Edom.
developments: Joab remained in Edom for six months to cut off every male (1 Kings 11:15-16)
Hadad flees with some of his father's Edomite servants (1 Kings 11:17)
He was a small child at the time of the escape (1 Kings 11:17)
They travel through Midian and Paran on their way to Egypt (1 Kings 11:18)
events.significance: Hadad’s survival was the seed of future trouble for the house of David.

events.title: Refuge and Favor in Egypt
events.summary: Hadad is welcomed by Pharaoh and eventually marries into the Egyptian royal family.
developments: Pharaoh gives Hadad a house, food, and land (1 Kings 11:18)
Hadad finds great favor in the sight of Pharaoh (1 Kings 11:19)
He marries the sister of Queen Tahpenes (1 Kings 11:19)
His son, Genubath, is raised in Pharaoh's palace among the king's sons (1 Kings 11:20)
events.significance: His high-level international connections made him a formidable political rival.

events.title: The Return to Edom
events.summary: Upon hearing of the deaths of David and Joab, Hadad requests permission to return to his homeland.
developments: Hadad learns in Egypt that the king and the commander of the army are dead (1 Kings 11:21)
He asks Pharaoh, 'Let me depart, that I may go to my own country' (1 Kings 11:21)
Pharaoh questions why he would leave such comfort (1 Kings 11:22)
Hadad insists, saying, 'No, but let me go anyway' (1 Kings 11:22)
events.significance: His return was driven by nationalistic duty and a desire for restoration.

events.title: The Adversary of Solomon
events.summary: God uses Hadad as a scourge to discipline Solomon for his idolatry.
developments: The Lord raised up an adversary against Solomon, Hadad the Edomite (1 Kings 11:14)
He is described as being of the royal house in Edom (1 Kings 11:14)
The text notes the 'mischief' or 'evil' that Hadad did (1 Kings 11:25)
He loathed Israel and reigned over Edom during Solomon's later years (1 Kings 11:25)
events.significance: Hadad represents the breaking of the 'Pax Salomonis' due to spiritual failure.

label: Hadadezer
overview: Ruled Zobah and fought against David. The son of Rehob, he lost troops, gold shields and bronze to David. He later summoned Aramean reinforcements, but after another defeat the kings under him made peace with Israel.

card.role: King of Zobah defeated by David

events.title: Loses troops and wealth to David after marching toward the Euphrates
Summons reinforcements, but his army loses and his subject kings submit to Israel

label: Hagar
overview: Egyptian maidservant of Sarah and mother of Abraham's son Ishmael. She fled Sarah's harsh treatment, and the Angel of the LORD told her to return. Later sent away with Ishmael, she received God's help when their water ran out.

details.label: Role
details.value: Sarah's maidservant, given to Abraham as a wife

events.title: Conceives by Abram and flees Sarai's harsh treatment
Meets the LORD's Angel and calls Him the God who sees her
Gives birth to Ishmael
Is sent away with her son after Sarah demands their removal
Runs out of water before God shows her a well
Finds an Egyptian wife for Ishmael

label: Haggai

details.label: Role

details.label: Named in
details.value: Messages delivered in Darius's second year

events.title: Rebukes neglect of the temple, and the leaders and people resume work
Delivers God's promise of greater glory for the temple and peace
Confronts the people's defilement and announces God's promise of blessing
Announces that God has chosen Zerubbabel to be like His signet ring
The temple is completed through the prophetic ministry of Haggai and Zechariah

label: Haman
overview: Rose above the other princes under King Xerxes and plotted to kill every Jew in the kingdom after Mordecai refused to bow to him. Esther exposed him, and he was hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai.

card.role: Official who plotted the Jews' destruction

details.label: Role
details.value: Official elevated above the other princes

details.label: Family
details.value: Son of Hammedatha; husband of Zeresh

events.title: Receives royal honor and plots against the Jews after Mordecai refuses to bow
Secures a royal decree to kill the Jews, including women and children
Has gallows built for Mordecai on Zeresh's and his friends' advice
Must parade Mordecai through the city in royal honor
Esther exposes him, and he is hanged on his own gallows

label: Hammuel
overview: Hammuel was a descendant of Simeon and a member of one of the leading families within that tribe. He is mentioned in the genealogical records of 1 Chronicles, which detail the lineage of the sons of Jacob. As a grandson of Shaul and the father of Zaccur, Hammuel represents the continuity of the Simeonite line during the period when the tribe was becoming increasingly integrated with the tribe of Judah. While his individual life is not the subject of a narrative, his inclusion in the sacred genealogies ensures that his place in the covenant family of Israel is preserved for posterity.

events.title: Ancestral Placement
events.summary: Hammuel is recorded in the official genealogy of the tribe of Simeon.
developments: He is listed as the son of Mishma (1 Chronicles 4:26)
His father Mishma was the son of Mibsam (1 Chronicles 4:25)
This line descends from Shaul, a son of the patriarch Simeon (1 Chronicles 4:24-25)
He is the father of Zaccur and the grandfather of Shimei (1 Chronicles 4:26-27)
events.significance: His placement in the record validates the legal and tribal standing of his descendants.

events.title: Prolific Descendants
events.summary: The family of Hammuel is noted for its growth and strength within the tribe.
developments: Hammuel's grandson Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters (1 Chronicles 4:27)
The record notes that most of the tribe of Simeon did not multiply as much as Judah (1 Chronicles 4:27)
Hammuel's line represents a significant exception of family growth (1 Chronicles 4:26-27)
His family dwelt in the southern regions of the land until the reign of David (1 Chronicles 4:28-31)
events.significance: Hammuel's lineage helped maintain the Simeonite presence in the south of Israel.

label: Hanamel
overview: Sold his field in Anathoth to his cousin Jeremiah for seventeen shekels of silver. He approached Jeremiah in the courtyard of the guard, just as the LORD had foretold, and witnessed the handover of the deed to Baruch.

card.role: Jeremiah's cousin who sold a field

label: Hanani (brother of Nehemiah)
overview: Nehemiah's brother who brought news of Jerusalem's broken walls and the returned exiles' distress. After the wall was rebuilt, Nehemiah put him in charge of Jerusalem alongside Hananiah, the fortress commander.

details.label: Role
details.value: Put in charge of Jerusalem with Hananiah

events.title: Reports Jerusalem's broken walls and the returned exiles' distress to Nehemiah
Receives charge of Jerusalem with Hananiah after the wall is rebuilt

label: Hanani (the seer)
overview: Rebuked King Asa of Judah for relying on Aram's king instead of the Lord. He told Asa that his foolish action would bring war. Asa became enraged and put him in prison.

label: Hananiah
overview: Hananiah is a name shared by several men in the Bible, most notably a false prophet who opposed Jeremiah and a faithful official who served under Nehemiah. The false prophet Hananiah famously broke Jeremiah’s wooden yoke and predicted a swift return from Babylonian exile, only to be struck dead for his lies. In contrast, the Hananiah in the book of Nehemiah was a 'faithful man who feared God more than many' and was given charge over the city of Jerusalem and its fortress. Additionally, the Hebrew name of Shadrach, one of the three youths in the fiery furnace, was Hananiah. These varied figures represent the spectrum of leadership, from the dangers of false prophecy to the vital importance of administrative integrity.

events.title: Conflict with Jeremiah
events.summary: Hananiah the prophet from Gibeon publicly contradicts Jeremiah’s message of a long exile.
developments: He declares that God will break the yoke of the king of Babylon within two years (Jeremiah 28:1-3)
He predicts the return of the Temple vessels and King Jehoiachin (Jeremiah 28:3-4)
Jeremiah says 'Amen' but warns that true prophets are known by their fulfillment (Jeremiah 28:5-9)
Hananiah takes the wooden yoke from Jeremiah's neck and breaks it (Jeremiah 28:10)
events.significance: Hananiah represents the popular but false hope that led to Judah’s final destruction.

events.title: Judgment of the False Prophet
events.summary: Jeremiah delivers a word from God announcing the death of Hananiah for his rebellion.
developments: God tells Jeremiah that Hananiah has replaced wooden bars with iron bars (Jeremiah 28:13-14)
Jeremiah tells Hananiah that God has not sent him and he has made the people trust a lie (Jeremiah 28:15)
He prophesies that Hananiah will die within the year (Jeremiah 28:16)
Hananiah dies in the seventh month of that same year (Jeremiah 28:17)
events.significance: His death served as a definitive sign of the authority of Jeremiah’s message.

events.title: Exile of the Hebrew Youth
events.summary: Another Hananiah is taken as a noble captive to Babylon and renamed Shadrach.
developments: He is among the youths of the royal family taken to the palace (Daniel 1:3-6)
The chief of the eunuchs gives him the name Shadrach (Daniel 1:7)
He joins Daniel in the ten-day test of vegetables and water (Daniel 1:11-14)
He is found ten times better than all the Babylonian wise men (Daniel 1:20)
events.significance: This Hananiah represents the faithful remnant that preserved their identity in a foreign land.

events.title: The Fiery Furnace
events.summary: Hananiah (Shadrach) refuses to bow to a golden image and is miraculously saved from fire.
developments: He and his two friends refuse to serve the king's gods (Daniel 3:12)
They declare that God is able to deliver them from the furnace (Daniel 3:17-18)
They are thrown into the furnace heated seven times hotter than normal (Daniel 3:19-23)
They emerge from the fire without even the smell of smoke (Daniel 3:27)
events.significance: His courage led to a royal decree honoring the God of Israel.

events.title: Governor of the Castle
events.summary: A third Hananiah is appointed by Nehemiah to oversee the security of Jerusalem.
developments: Nehemiah gives Hananiah charge over the castle (Nehemiah 7:2)
He is described as a 'faithful man who feared God more than many' (Nehemiah 7:2)
He is tasked with managing the gates and the guards (Nehemiah 7:3)
He served alongside Hanani, Nehemiah’s brother (Nehemiah 7:2)
events.significance: He represents the godly administrative leadership required to maintain the restoration.

label: Hannah
overview: Mother of Samuel who prayed for a son while Peninnah taunted her for having no children. She vowed to dedicate him to the LORD and brought him to Eli after he was weaned. She later had three more sons and two daughters.

details.label: Family

events.title: Prays for a son and vows to dedicate him to the LORD
Gives birth to Samuel after the LORD remembers her
Brings Samuel to Eli at Shiloh and praises the LORD in prayer
Brings Samuel a robe each year and has five more children

label: Hanun
overview: Succeeded his father Nahash as king of Ammon. He humiliated David's messengers by shaving half their beards and cutting their clothes, then hired military help as Ammon prepared for war with Israel.

card.role: Ammonite king who humiliated David's messengers

events.title: Succeeds Nahash and humiliates David's messengers after hearing his advisers' accusations
Hires chariots and horsemen with the Ammonites to prepare for war

label: Hathach
overview: Royal eunuch appointed to attend Esther. He carried messages between her and Mordecai after the decree to destroy the Jews, bringing her Mordecai's report and his appeal that she plead with the king.

details.label: Role
details.value: One of the king's eunuchs, appointed to Esther

label: Hazael
overview: Became king of Aram after killing his master Ben-hadad with a wet cloth over his face. Elisha had foretold his kingship and the atrocities he would commit. He took Israelite territory and oppressed Israel throughout Jehoahaz's reign.

card.role: King of Aram who oppressed Israel

details.label: Family
details.value: Father of Ben-hadad, who succeeded him

events.title: Hears Elisha foretell his kingship and violence against Israel
Kills Ben-hadad with a wet cloth and becomes king
Defeats Israel across its territory east of the Jordan
Captures Gath and withdraws from Jerusalem after Joash sends valuables
Dies after oppressing Israel, and his son Ben-hadad becomes king

label: Heldai
overview: Heldai is a name mentioned in the post-exilic period as one of the faithful Jews who returned from Babylon with gifts for the reconstruction of the Temple. In a significant prophetic act, the prophet Zechariah was commanded to take silver and gold from Heldai and others to fashion a crown for the High Priest Joshua. This crown was then kept in the Temple as a memorial to Heldai’s devotion. Another Heldai was a captain in David’s army, a Netophathite who led a division of 24,000 men during the twelfth month. Both figures represent the quiet but essential support that sustains the spiritual and military life of the nation.

events.title: Commander in David's Army
events.summary: Heldai is appointed as a leader over a major division of the military.
developments: He is identified as Heldai the Netophathite, of the family of Othniel (1 Chronicles 27:15)
He leads the twelfth division of 24,000 men (1 Chronicles 27:15)
His division is assigned to the twelfth month (1 Chronicles 27:15)
His descent from Othniel (the first judge) gave him high social standing (1 Chronicles 27:15)
events.significance: Heldai provided administrative and military stability during the peak of the United Monarchy.

events.title: Contributor from the Exile
events.summary: A different Heldai returns from Babylon with resources for the Temple restoration.
developments: He arrives in Jerusalem with a group from the captivity (Zechariah 6:10)
He brings silver and gold as a gift for the house of the Lord (Zechariah 6:10)
The prophet is told to collect the metals that day (Zechariah 6:10)
Heldai is listed alongside Tobijah and Jedaiah (Zechariah 6:10)
events.significance: He represents the continued dedication of the exiles to the restoration of Jerusalem.

events.title: The Memorial Crown
events.summary: Heldai’s gift is used to create a prophetic crown that honors his name.
developments: Zechariah makes a crown to set on the head of Joshua the High Priest (Zechariah 6:11)
The crown is then placed in the Temple (Zechariah 6:14)
It is designated as a memorial for Helem (an alternate name for Heldai) (Zechariah 6:14)
The crown remains a visual sign of the coming 'Branch' who will be both King and Priest (Zechariah 6:12-13)
events.significance: Heldai’s generosity was immortalized as a permanent part of the Temple’s prophetic witness.

label: Heman
overview: A Kohathite singer whom David put in charge of music in God's house. He played bronze cymbals, was called the king's seer, and directed his sons in music for worship.

details.label: Family

card.note: The Bible doesn't say whether he is Heman the Ezrahite named in Psalm 88 or the Heman compared with Solomon in 1 Kings 4:31.

events.title: Is appointed to sound bronze cymbals with Asaph and Ethan
Directs his sons in music under the king's authority

label: Herod Agrippa I
overview: King who killed James, John's brother, and imprisoned Peter. After Peter escaped, he ordered the guards executed. An angel struck him for failing to give glory to God when a crowd called his speech a god's voice; he died, eaten by worms.

card.role: King who persecuted the Jerusalem church

events.title: Has James killed and arrests Peter during the Feast of Unleavened Bread
Fails to find Peter and orders the guards executed
Fails to glorify God and dies after an angel strikes him

label: Herod Antipas
overview: Ruled Galilee as tetrarch and imprisoned John the Baptist after John condemned his marriage to Herodias. He ordered John's beheading after a birthday oath, and later mocked Jesus before returning Him to Pilate.

card.role: Tetrarch of Galilee who executed John

details.label: Family
details.value: Married Herodias, his brother Philip's wife

events.title: Imprisons John after John condemns his marriage
Orders John's beheading after Herodias' daughter claims his birthday promise
Questions and mocks Jesus, then sends Him back to Pilate

label: Herod the Great
overview: Ruled Judea when Jesus was born. After the Magi did not return to him, he ordered the killing of boys aged two and under in and around Bethlehem. Joseph had taken Jesus and Mary to Egypt after an angel's warning.

card.role: King who ordered Bethlehem's child killings

events.title: Questions the Magi and sends them to search for Jesus in Bethlehem
Orders boys killed in Bethlehem after the Magi avoid him
Dies and is succeeded in Judea by Archelaus

label: Herodians
overview: The Herodians were a political faction in first-century Judea who supported the Roman-appointed dynasty of Herod and the continuation of Roman rule. While they generally differed from the Pharisees on matters of Jewish law and tradition, the two groups frequently joined forces in their mutual opposition to Jesus, whom they both viewed as a threat to their respective authority. The Herodians notably participated in a failed attempt to trap Jesus with a question about paying taxes to Caesar. Their presence in the Gospels highlights the intense political and religious pressure Jesus faced from those who sought to preserve the status quo.

events.title: The Conspiracy of Enemies
events.summary: The Herodians first appear in an unlikely alliance with the Pharisees to plot against Jesus.
developments: Jesus heals a man with a withered hand on the Sabbath (Mark 3:1-5)
The Pharisees immediately go out to meet with the Herodians (Mark 3:6)
They consult together how they might destroy Him (Mark 3:6)
This union was significant because the two groups were usually political rivals (Mark 3:6)
events.significance: Their coalition demonstrated that Jesus’ influence was so great it unified opposing political parties.

events.title: The Leaven of Herod
events.summary: Jesus warns His disciples against the corrupting influence of the Herodians.
developments: Jesus warns the disciples to 'Watch out; beware of the leaven of the Pharisees' (Mark 8:15)
He adds, 'and the leaven of Herod' (Mark 8:15)
Leaven represents a pervasive, corrupting philosophy or attitude (Mark 8:15)
The disciples mistakenly think He is talking about physical bread (Mark 8:16-21)
events.significance: Jesus identified the Herodians as a primary spiritual and moral danger to His followers.

events.title: The Tax Trap
events.summary: Herodians and Pharisees attempt to force Jesus into a legal dilemma regarding Roman taxes.
developments: They send their disciples with the Herodians to Jesus (Matthew 22:16)
They begin with false flattery about His truthfulness (Matthew 22:16)
They ask, 'Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?' (Matthew 22:17)
If He said no, the Herodians would report Him for treason; if yes, the people would turn on Him (Matthew 22:15-17)
events.significance: The Herodians were the specific agents used to try and criminalize Jesus under Roman law.

events.title: The Rebuttal
events.summary: Jesus outmaneuvers the Herodians with His famous teaching on the image of God.
developments: Jesus perceives their malice and calls them hypocrites (Matthew 22:18)
He asks for a denarius and points out Caesar's likeness and inscription (Matthew 22:19-20)
He commands, 'Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's' (Matthew 22:21)
The Herodians are left in awe and depart from Him (Matthew 22:22)
events.significance: This response established the biblical principle of dual citizenship and limited government.

label: Herodias
overview: Philip's wife, whom his brother Herod married. After John the Baptist called the marriage unlawful, she wanted him dead and told her daughter to ask Herod for John's head.

card.role: Herod's wife who sought John's death

details.label: Family
details.value: Philip's wife, whom his brother Herod married; mother of a daughter

events.title: Holds a grudge against John after he condemns her marriage to Herod
Tells her daughter to request John's head and receives it after his execution

label: Hezekiah
overview: Ruled Judah for twenty-nine years, removed idols and trusted the LORD when Assyria threatened Jerusalem. God answered his prayers for deliverance and healing. He showed Babylonian envoys his treasures; he also became proud but humbled himself.

card.role: King of Judah who opposed idolatry

details.label: Role
details.value: King of Judah for twenty-nine years

details.label: Family
details.value: Son of Ahaz and Abi; father of Manasseh

events.title: Begins ruling Judah and destroys idols, including the bronze snake
Reopens the temple and orders its purification
Invites Israel and Judah to celebrate Passover in Jerusalem
Prays over Assyria's threat, and the LORD's angel strikes the Assyrian camp
Prays during a deadly illness, and God promises him fifteen more years
Shows Babylon's envoys his treasures and hears Isaiah's warning of exile
Humbles himself after pride brings wrath on him, Judah and Jerusalem
Dies honored by Judah and Jerusalem; Manasseh succeeds him

label: Hezron
overview: Hezron was the grandson of the patriarch Judah and a foundational figure in the genealogy of the Davidic dynasty. Born to Perez after the family migrated to Egypt, Hezron became the head of a major clan within the tribe of Judah. His name is central to the biblical record of the Messianic line, appearing in both the Old Testament genealogies and the New Testament lineages of Jesus Christ. Hezron represents the continuity of God's promise to Judah during the long centuries of the Egyptian sojourn.

events.title: Migration to Egypt
events.summary: Hezron is listed among the descendants of Jacob who settle in Egypt during the famine.
developments: He is the son of Perez, of the tribe of Judah (Genesis 46:12)
He enters Egypt with his brother Hamul (Genesis 46:12)
He is part of the 'seventy souls' of the house of Jacob (Genesis 46:27)
He is born into the line that held the scepter promise (Genesis 49:10)
events.significance: Hezron was a first-generation exile in the land of Goshen.

events.title: The Sons of Hezron
events.summary: The genealogy of Hezron is recorded at length to establish the noble families of Judah.
developments: He has three primary sons: Jerahmeel, Ram, and Chelubai (Caleb) (1 Chronicles 2:9)
Through Ram, he becomes the ancestor of the royal house (1 Chronicles 2:10)
He marries a daughter of Machir, the father of Gilead, at age sixty (1 Chronicles 2:21)
This marriage linked the tribe of Judah to the influential clans of Manasseh (1 Chronicles 2:21-23)
events.significance: Hezron was a bridge-builder between major tribal lineages.

events.title: The Hezronite Clan
events.summary: During the wilderness census, the descendants of Hezron are recognized as a distinct and large family.
developments: The clan is officially named 'the Hezronites' (Numbers 26:6)
They are part of the total strength of the tribe of Judah (Numbers 26:22)
The family maintained its identity through the 400 years in Egypt (Numbers 26:1-22)
Hezron’s line is singled out for its legal and genealogical importance (1 Chronicles 2:5-25)
events.significance: The clan's survival ensured the preservation of the royal seed.

events.title: Link to the Messiah
events.summary: Hezron is permanently recorded as a direct ancestor of King David and Jesus Christ.
developments: He is the father of Ram and the grandfather of Amminadab (Ruth 4:19)
He is listed in the genealogy of the Book of Ruth (Ruth 4:18-22)
Matthew includes 'Esrom' (Hezron) in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:3)
Luke also traces the ancestry of Jesus through Hezron back to Adam (Luke 3:33)
events.significance: His placement in the genealogy validates the fulfillment of God's promise to Judah.

label: Hilkiah
overview: Found the Book of the Law in the temple while serving as high priest under Josiah. He gave it to Shaphan and joined the delegation that consulted Huldah. Josiah later ordered him to remove articles made for other gods from the temple.

card.role: Josiah's high priest who found Scripture

events.title: Finds the Book of the Law and gives it to Shaphan
Consults Huldah with the delegation sent by Josiah
Receives orders to remove articles made for other gods from the temple

label: Hiram
overview: King of Tyre and a friend of David. He supplied workers and cedar for David's palace, made a treaty with Solomon, and supplied timber and a craftsman for Solomon's building work.

events.title: Sends cedar, carpenters and stonemasons to build David's palace
Agrees to supply temple timber and makes a treaty with Solomon
Sends the craftsman Huram-abi to work with Solomon's craftsmen
Inspects Solomon's gift of twenty towns and finds them unsatisfactory
Sends experienced sailors to serve with Solomon's men on a voyage to Ophir

label: Holy Spirit
overview: The Holy Spirit is the third Person of the Trinity, identified as the presence and power of God active in the world and within believers. In the Old Testament, the Spirit came upon specific individuals—prophets, kings, and craftsmen—for particular tasks or messages. The New Testament records a transition at Pentecost, where the Spirit was poured out on all believers to dwell within them permanently. Described as the 'Counselor,' 'Comforter,' and 'Spirit of Truth,' He is responsible for convicting of sin, guiding into truth, and empowering the church for global mission. The Holy Spirit is the divine agent of transformation, producing spiritual fruit and distributing gifts for the building up of the body of Christ.

events.title: The Spirit in Creation
events.summary: The Holy Spirit is present at the very beginning of the biblical narrative.
developments: The Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters (Genesis 1:2)
He is the agent of life and order in the initial void (Genesis 1:2)
God breathes the 'breath of life' into man, often linked to the Spirit (Genesis 2:7)
Elihu later says, 'The Spirit of God has made me' (Job 33:4)
events.significance: This establishes the Spirit as an eternal participant in the work of the Godhead.

events.title: Empowering for Specific Tasks
events.summary: In the Old Testament, the Spirit 'clothes' or 'fills' individuals for special service.
developments: The Spirit fills Bezalel with skill for the Tabernacle (Exodus 31:3)
The Spirit of the Lord takes possession of Gideon (Judges 6:34)
He rushes upon Samson, granting him supernatural strength (Judges 14:6, 19)
The Spirit comes upon Saul and later David when they are anointed (1 Samuel 10:10, 16:13)
events.significance: Divine empowerment was selective and task-oriented during the Old Covenant.

events.title: Prophecy of the New Spirit
events.summary: The prophets predict a future day when the Spirit will be given to everyone and transform the heart.
developments: Joel prophesies that God will pour out His Spirit on 'all flesh' (Joel 2:28)
He says sons and daughters will prophesy (Joel 2:28)
Ezekiel promises God will put a 'new spirit' within His people (Ezekiel 36:26)
The Spirit will cause the people to walk in God's statutes (Ezekiel 36:27)
events.significance: This created the Messianic expectation of universal spiritual restoration.

events.title: The Spirit and the Messiah
events.summary: The Holy Spirit is the primary agent in the birth and public ministry of Jesus.
developments: Jesus is conceived in Mary by the Holy Spirit (Matthew 1:18-20)
The Spirit descends like a dove upon Jesus at His baptism (Matthew 3:16)
Jesus is led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted (Matthew 4:1)
He returns in the power of the Spirit to Galilee (Luke 4:14)
events.significance: Jesus was the first person to perfectly and permanently possess the fullness of the Spirit.

events.title: The Promised Counselor
events.summary: During the Last Supper, Jesus promises to send the Spirit to take His place.
developments: He calls the Spirit the 'Counselor' or 'Advocate' (John 14:16)
The Spirit will teach the disciples and remind them of Jesus' words (John 14:26)
He will bear witness about Jesus to the world (John 15:26)
The Spirit will convict the world of sin, righteousness, and judgment (John 16:8)
events.significance: The Spirit became the personal presence of God within the church.

events.title: The Day of Pentecost
events.summary: The Holy Spirit is poured out on the church, fulfilling the ancient prophecies.
developments: A sound like a mighty rushing wind fills the house (Acts 2:2)
Tongues as of fire rest on each of the 120 disciples (Acts 2:3)
They are all filled with the Spirit and speak in other tongues (Acts 2:4)
Peter declares this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel (Acts 2:16-21)
events.significance: Pentecost marked the official birth of the global, Spirit-led church.

events.title: Expanding the Boundaries
events.summary: The Spirit moves through the apostles to include Samaritans and Gentiles in the church.
developments: Samaritans receive the Spirit when Peter and John lay hands on them (Acts 8:14-17)
The Spirit falls on Cornelius and his household while Peter is preaching (Acts 10:44)
This 'Gentile Pentecost' proves that God shows no partiality (Acts 10:45-47)
The Spirit is the engine of the gospel’s spread to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8)
events.significance: The Holy Spirit was the final authority in settling the church’s ethnic inclusiveness.

events.title: Gifts and Fruit
events.summary: The Apostle Paul explains how the Spirit operates within the individual believer and the body.
developments: The Spirit distributes diverse gifts to each member for the common good (1 Corinthians 12:4-11)
He produces the 'fruit of the Spirit'—love, joy, peace, etc. (Galatians 5:22-23)
The Spirit seals the believer for the day of redemption (Ephesians 1:13-14)
He intercedes for the saints with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26-27)
events.significance: The Spirit is the source of both the church's supernatural power and its moral character.

label: Hophni

Buys his wife for silver and barley after God's command to love her again

overview: Ruled Israel in Samaria for nine years after murdering Pekah. He paid tribute to Assyria, then withheld it and sent messengers to Egypt. Assyria imprisoned him, and Samaria fell in his ninth year, with Israelites taken into exile.

details.label: Role

label: Ithiel
overview: Ithiel is a name mentioned in two distinct contexts in the Hebrew Bible. The first appears in the genealogies of the tribe of Benjamin, identifying him as a son of Jeshaiah and an ancestor of Sallu, one of the first leaders to resettle in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. The second occurrence is found in the enigmatic opening of Proverbs 30, where the sage Agur addresses his words to 'Ithiel and Ucal.' In this wisdom context, Ithiel may be a personal name for a disciple of Agur, or according to some interpretations, a symbolic name meaning 'God is with me.' Both instances highlight the name’s association with post-exilic leadership and the search for divine wisdom.

label: Jabin
overview: Jabin was a title or name held by powerful Canaanite kings who ruled from the strategic northern city of Hazor. One King Jabin led a massive coalition of northern kings against Joshua, only to be defeated and have his city burned. Generations later, another Jabin, described as the 'king of Canaan,' oppressed Israel for twenty years with a formidable force of 900 iron chariots. His reign was characterized by harsh military dominance until the prophetess Deborah and the commander Barak mobilized the tribes. The defeat of Jabin’s general, Sisera, led to the total destruction of Jabin’s power, marking the end of Canaanite hegemony in the north.

events.title: The Northern Coalition

events.significance: Jabin was the leader of the final major organized resistance in Canaan.

He strikes Jabin with the sword (Joshua 11:10)
The city of Hazor is burned with fire (Joshua 11:11)
This fulfilled the command of the Lord regarding the devoted cities (Joshua 11:12)
events.significance: The death of this Jabin symbolized the collapse of Canaanite political structure.

events.title: The Second Jabin's Oppression

His commander is Sisera, who dwells in Harosheth-hagoyim (Judges 4:2)
Jabin possesses 900 chariots of iron (Judges 4:3)

events.significance: Jabin represents the 'rebounding' of pagan power when Israel abandoned the covenant.

events.title: Collapse of the Military Force

developments: Barak and Deborah lead the Israelite counter-attack (Judges 4:14)
The Lord routs Sisera and all his chariots before Barak (Judges 4:15)
Not a single man of Jabin’s host is left alive (Judges 4:16)
Sisera is killed by Jael, removing Jabin's chief support (Judges 4:21)
events.significance: The loss of his army left Jabin defenseless against the rising Israelite power.

events.title: The End of the Canaanite Kingdom
events.summary: Following the battle, the Israelites systematically dismantle Jabin’s remaining authority.
developments: The hand of the people of Israel pressed harder and harder against Jabin (Judges 4:24)

label: Jair
overview: Jair was a prominent leader and judge of Israel from the region of Gilead who led the nation for twenty-two years. He is primarily known for his thirty sons, who were influential enough to ride on thirty donkeys and possess thirty distinct cities in Gilead, known as Havvoth-jair. Jair’s judgeship followed that of Tola and occurred during a period of relative expansion and tribal stability in the Transjordan. He was eventually buried in the city of Kamon, leaving a legacy of family prosperity and territorial development. The name Jair was also held by an earlier descendant of Manasseh who captured several villages during the initial conquest.

label: Jehoahaz
overview: Jehoahaz was the name of several kings, most notably the son of Jehu who reigned over Israel and the son of Josiah who briefly ruled Judah. Jehoahaz of Israel presided over a period of extreme national weakness, as the Aramean King Hazael decimated the Israelite army and oppressed the land. Despite his continued idolatry, Jehoahaz eventually sought the Lord, and God provided a 'deliverer' to relieve the Syrian pressure. Jehoahaz of Judah, also known as Shallum, reigned for only three months after his father’s death at Megiddo. He was deposed and taken into exile by Pharaoh Neco, becoming a symbol of the end of Judean independence.

label: Jehoash
overview: Jehoash (also known as Joash) was the name of two prominent kings: the survivor of the Davidic line in Judah and a successful military ruler of Israel. Jehoash of Judah was hidden in the Temple as an infant to escape the purge of Athaliah and was later crowned at age seven through the courage of the high priest Jehoiada. His early reign was marked by significant Temple repairs, though his later years saw a spiritual decline after Jehoiada’s death. Jehoash of Israel was noted for his three victories over Syria, fulfilling the final prophecy of Elisha, and for his humiliating defeat of Judah, which resulted in the looting of Jerusalem. Both kings represent the complicated and often violent history of the divided kingdoms.

details.value: King of Judah for eleven years

details.label: Also called
details.value: Eliakim before Pharaoh Neco renamed him

details.label: Family
details.value: Son of Josiah and Zebidah; father of Jehoiachin

events.title: Is installed and renamed by Neco, then taxes Judah to pay him
Has the prophet Uriah brought back from Egypt and kills him
Burns Jeremiah's scroll and orders Jeremiah and Baruch arrested
Rebels after serving Nebuchadnezzar for three years
Dies and is succeeded by his son Jehoiachin

label: Jehonadab
overview: Rode with Jehu and accompanied him into Baal's temple. The son of Rechab, also called Jonadab, he commanded his descendants to avoid wine, houses and farming and to live in tents. His descendants still obeyed those commands in Jeremiah's time.

card.role: Rechab's son who commanded tent living

details.label: Family
details.value: Son of Rechab; forefather of the Rechabites

events.title: Joins Jehu in his chariot
Enters Baal's temple with Jehu before Jehu orders the worshipers killed
His descendants recount and obey his commands to avoid wine and live in tents

label: Jehoram
overview: Jehoram (also known as Joram) was the name of two contemporary kings whose reigns brought the kingdoms of Israel and Judah into a disastrous spiritual and political alliance. Jehoram of Judah, the son of Jehoshaphat, married the daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, leading Judah into intense idolatry and murdering his own brothers. His reign ended in military humiliation and a horrific terminal illness. Jehoram of Israel, the last of the house of Omri, struggled through numerous wars with Syria and the Moabite rebellion, eventually being assassinated by Jehu. Both kings represent the dark peak of the house of Ahab’s influence and the eventual violent fulfillment of God’s judgment against that dynasty.

events.title: Accession and Fratricide
events.summary: Jehoram of Judah begins his reign by eliminating all his royal brothers to secure his throne.
developments: He is the firstborn son of Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 21:3)
As soon as he had established himself, he killed all his brothers with the sword (2 Chronicles 21:4)
He also executed some of the other princes of Israel (2 Chronicles 21:4)
He married Athaliah, the daughter of Ahab (2 Chronicles 21:6)
events.significance: This act introduced a level of internal violence previously unseen in the Davidic line.

events.title: Jehoram of Israel and the Moabite War
events.summary: In the north, Jehoram succeeds his brother Ahaziah and attempts to retake Moab.
developments: Mesha, King of Moab, rebels after Ahab’s death (2 Kings 3:4-5)
Jehoram forms a coalition with Judah and Edom (2 Kings 3:6-9)
The army nearly dies of thirst in the wilderness (2 Kings 3:9)
Elisha provides a miraculous supply of water but prophesies a bittersweet victory (2 Kings 3:16-19)
events.significance: His reign was marked by constant struggle to maintain the Omride empire.

events.title: The Letter from Elijah
events.summary: Jehoram of Judah receives a written prophecy of judgment from Elijah for his wickedness.
developments: A letter arrives from the prophet Elijah condemning his idolatry (2 Chronicles 21:12)
He is rebuked for leading Judah into 'whoring' as the house of Ahab did (2 Chronicles 21:13)
Elijah predicts a great plague on his people, family, and possessions (2 Chronicles 21:14)
He is told he will suffer a severe intestinal disease (2 Chronicles 21:15)
events.significance: This was the only recorded interaction between Elijah and a king of Judah.

events.title: Rebellion and Raid
events.summary: Jehoram of Judah loses control of his vassals and suffers a devastating palace raid.
developments: Edom revolts against Judean rule and sets up its own king (2 Kings 8:20)
Philistines and Arabians invade and plunder the king’s house (2 Chronicles 21:16-17)
They carry away all the king's sons and wives except Jehoahaz (2 Chronicles 21:17)
The kingdom shrinks significantly in size and power (2 Kings 8:22)
events.significance: The military losses were seen as the direct result of Jehoram’s abandonment of God.

events.title: The Death of Jehoram of Judah
events.summary: He dies in extreme pain from the predicted disease and is buried without honor.
developments: The Lord struck him with an incurable bowel disease (2 Chronicles 21:18)
After two years, his bowels came out because of the disease (2 Chronicles 21:19)
The text says he 'departed with no one's regret' (2 Chronicles 21:20)
He was buried in the City of David but not in the tombs of the kings (2 Chronicles 21:20)
events.significance: His ignoble end was the definitive biblical example of a cursed reign.

events.title: The Assassination of Jehoram of Israel
events.summary: The last king of Ahab's house is executed by Jehu at the vineyard of Naboth.
developments: Jehoram is wounded in battle with the Syrians at Ramoth-gilead (2 Kings 9:14-15)
Jehu rides to Jezreel and meets Jehoram in the field (2 Kings 9:21)
Jehoram asks 'Is it peace, Jehu?' and Jehu rebukes him for Jezebel's sorceries (2 Kings 9:22)
Jehu draws his bow and strikes Jehoram through the heart (2 Kings 9:24)
events.significance: His death marked the total and violent collapse of the Omride dynasty in Israel.

label: Jehoshaphat
overview: Ruled Judah for twenty-five years and sent teachers of the LORD's Law through its towns. He sought God when enemies invaded, and the LORD defeated them. His alliances with Ahab and Ahaziah also brought prophetic rebukes and judgment.

card.role: King of Judah, son of Asa

details.label: Role
details.value: King of Judah for twenty-five years

events.title: Sends officials, Levites and priests to teach the Law throughout Judah
Goes to battle with Ahab and cries out as enemy chariots pursue him
Jehu rebukes him for helping the wicked
Calls the people back to the LORD and appoints judges
Seeks the LORD with Judah, and enemy armies destroy one another
Allies with Ahaziah to build ships, which the LORD destroys

label: Jehovah
overview: Jehovah is an English vocalization of the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter sacred name of God (YHWH) revealed to Moses at the burning bush. Derived from the Hebrew verb meaning 'to be,' the name signifies God's eternal, self-existent, and unchangeable nature. In most English translations, the name is rendered as 'the LORD' out of reverence for the Jewish tradition of not pronouncing the name aloud. Jehovah is the name associated with God’s covenant-keeping faithfulness, His presence with His people, and His role as the absolute Sovereign over history. In the biblical narrative, this name distinguishes the true God of Israel from the nameless and powerless idols of the surrounding nations.

events.title: Revelation at the Bush
events.summary: God reveals His personal name to Moses, establishing His eternal presence.
developments: Moses asks God for His name to tell the Israelites (Exodus 3:13)
God declares: 'I AM WHO I AM' (Exodus 3:14)
He identifies Himself as 'The Lord (YHWH), the God of your fathers' (Exodus 3:15)
He states this is His name forever, a memorial for all generations (Exodus 3:15)
events.significance: This revelation provided the foundation for Israel's unique monotheistic identity.

events.title: The Covenant Name
events.summary: God explains that the patriarchs knew Him as God Almighty, but He is now revealing the full weight of His name YHWH.
developments: God says He appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as El Shaddai (Exodus 6:3)
He states that by His name 'The Lord' (YHWH) He was not fully known to them (Exodus 6:3)
He links the name to the promise of delivering Israel from Egypt (Exodus 6:6-7)
The name becomes the guarantee of the Exodus (Exodus 6:2-8)
events.significance: Jehovah became the active, 'performing' name of God in the deliverance of the nation.

events.title: The Third Commandment
events.summary: The Law establishes the absolute sanctity and reverence required for God's name.
developments: God commands, 'You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain' (Exodus 20:7)
The penalty is stated: the Lord will not hold him guiltless (Exodus 20:7)
This led to the later tradition of replacing the name with 'Adonai' (Lord) in speech (Exodus 20:7)
The name was to be honored as an extension of God’s own person (Leviticus 24:16)
events.significance: The name was treated as a holy and powerful object of worship.

events.title: Proclamation of Character
events.summary: God passes before Moses and proclaims the internal meaning of His name.
developments: The Lord descends in the cloud and stands with Moses (Exodus 34:5)
He proclaims the name: 'The Lord, the Lord' (YHWH, YHWH) (Exodus 34:6)
He defines the name as merciful, gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in love (Exodus 34:6)
He emphasizes His justice andHis clearing of the guilty (Exodus 34:7)
events.significance: This defined Jehovah not just as a power, but as a moral and relational Being.

events.title: The Priestly Blessing
events.summary: God instructs the priests to 'put His name' upon the people through a specific benediction.
developments: The Lord tells Moses how Aaron should bless the people (Numbers 6:22-23)
The blessing invokes the name of the Lord three times (Numbers 6:24-26)
God says, 'So shall they put my name upon the people' (Numbers 6:27)
The presence of the name is equated with the bestowal of peace (Numbers 6:27)
events.significance: The name Jehovah served as the spiritual 'seal' of protection for the nation.

events.title: Victory in the Name
events.summary: David defeats Goliath by relying solely on the authority and power of the name of Jehovah.
developments: David tells the giant he comes in the name of the Lord of hosts (1 Samuel 17:45)
He contrasts the giant’s physical weapons with the spiritual weight of the name (1 Samuel 17:45)
He declares the battle belongs to the Lord (1 Samuel 17:47)
The victory proves that 'there is a God in Israel' (1 Samuel 17:46)
events.significance: The name of God was the primary offensive weapon of the faithful.

events.title: Personal and Sovereign Title
events.summary: The Psalms celebrate Jehovah as the personal Shepherd and the supreme Ruler of the earth.
developments: David declares, 'The Lord (Jehovah) is my shepherd' (Psalm 23:1)
The psalmist asks God to judge the nations so they know His name is the Lord (Psalm 83:18)
He is called the 'Most High over all the earth' (Psalm 83:18)
His name is described as a 'strong tower' where the righteous run and are safe (Proverbs 18:10)
events.significance: The name became the center of personal devotion and national security.

label: Jehu
overview: King of Israel for twenty-eight years who destroyed Ahab's house and killed Baal's worshipers. God promised four generations of kings from his sons, but Jehu kept worshiping Jeroboam's golden calves.

card.role: King of Israel who killed Joram

details.label: Family
details.value: Son of Jehoshaphat, grandson of Nimshi; father of Jehoahaz

events.title: Elisha's messenger anoints him king and commands him to destroy Ahab's house
Kills Joram and orders the attack that leads to Ahaziah's death
Orders Jezebel thrown from a window, and dogs devour her body
Demands the heads of Ahab's seventy sons and kills those remaining in Jezreel
Has forty-two relatives of Ahaziah killed at Beth-eked
Takes Jehonadab into his chariot and destroys Ahab's remaining family in Samaria
Traps Baal's worshipers in their temple, has them killed and destroys the temple
Receives God's promise for his sons but continues the golden calf worship
Dies after twenty-eight years as king, and Jehoahaz succeeds him
God later announces judgment on his house for the bloodshed of Jezreel

label: Jephthah
overview: Defeated Ammon and judged Israel for six years. His only daughter met him on his return, and he carried out his burnt-offering vow. He also led Gilead against Ephraim in fighting that left 42,000 Ephraimites dead.

card.role: Judge who made a burnt-offering vow

details.label: Role

details.label: Family

details.label: Buried
details.value: One of the cities of Gilead

events.title: Is expelled by his brothers and settles in Tob
Returns at Gilead's request and becomes its leader and commander
Vows a burnt offering of whatever greets him from his house after victory
Defeats the Ammonites as the Lord gives him victory
His only daughter greets him, then asks for two months to mourn her virginity
Carries out his vow when his daughter returns after two months
Leads Gilead against Ephraim in fighting that leaves 42,000 Ephraimites dead
Dies after judging Israel for six years

label: Jeremiah
overview: Warned Judah of God's judgment and announced His promise of a new covenant. A priest from Anathoth, he faced death threats and imprisonment, including a muddy cistern. After Jerusalem fell, he stayed in Judah before being taken to Egypt.

details.label: Role

events.title: God calls him to speak to nations despite his objection that he is young
Faces death threats after warning that the temple will become like Shiloh
Dictates God's words to Baruch and replaces the scroll Jehoiakim burns
Confronts Hananiah's false message and predicts his death that year
Announces God's new covenant, with His law written on hearts and sins forgiven
Buys Hanamel's field and orders the deeds preserved for future restoration
Sinks into a muddy cistern and is rescued by Ebed-melech
Is released at Ramah and stays with Gedaliah in Judah
Is taken to Egypt with Baruch when the leaders reject God's command

label: Jeroboam
overview: Ruled Israel for twenty-two years after the kingdom divided. Jeroboam set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan and led Israel into sin. Ahijah announced the destruction of his household because of his sins.

card.role: King of Israel, son of Nebat

details.label: Role
details.value: King of Israel for twenty-two years

events.title: Serves Solomon over Joseph's labor force but rebels against him
Ahijah gives him ten pieces of a cloak, promising ten tribes
Israel makes him king after his return
Sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan, leading Israel into sin
His hand withers at Bethel and is restored after the prophet prays
Sends his wife to Ahijah, who announces judgment; their son Abijah dies
Dies after twenty-two years, and Nadab succeeds him

label: Jeroboam II
overview: Ruled Israel from Samaria for forty-one years. He restored Israel's boundary as Jonah had prophesied, but continued the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat. During his reign, Amos announced judgment against his house.

Restores Israel's boundary from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah

Dies and is succeeded by his son Zechariah

label: Jeshua
overview: High priest, son of Jozadak, who worked with Zerubbabel to rebuild the altar and temple. Zechariah saw him in a vision receiving clean garments as his iniquity was removed. The LORD also instructed Zechariah to place a crown on his head.

events.title: Rebuilds the altar with Zerubbabel and offers burnt offerings
Joins in appointing Levites to oversee temple construction
Resumes building with Zerubbabel, supported by Haggai and Zechariah
Receives clean garments in Zechariah's vision as his iniquity is removed
Is named to receive a crown as Zechariah announces the Branch

label: Jesse
overview: Father of David and son of Obed, from Bethlehem in Judah. He presented his sons to Samuel, who anointed David, the youngest. Later, he sent David with food for his brothers in Saul's army and stayed in Moab under the king's care.

details.label: Family
details.value: Son of Obed; father of eight sons, including David
