Sends David with food and asks for news of his brothers
David places him and his wife in the care of Moab's king

label: Jesus
overview: Son of God and Christ, born in Bethlehem. He proclaimed God's kingdom, healed the sick, and died for sins by crucifixion under Pilate. He rose on the third day and ascended to heaven after commissioning His witnesses.

card.role: Son of God, Christ and Savior

details.label: Role
details.value: Christ, Son of God and Savior

details.label: From
details.value: Born in Bethlehem; came from Nazareth in Galilee

details.label: Family
details.value: Born to Mary, wife of Joseph

events.title: Is born in Bethlehem and announced as Savior and Christ
Is baptized by John as the Father calls Him His beloved Son
Is tempted by Satan in the wilderness
Proclaims God's kingdom, calls disciples, and heals the sick
Hears Peter confess Him as Christ and foretells His death and resurrection
Rides into Jerusalem as the crowd welcomes Him
Shares bread and the cup, speaking of His blood of the covenant
Is betrayed by Judas and arrested
Is handed over for crucifixion by Pilate and dies
Rises from the dead on the third day
Commissions His witnesses and ascends to heaven

label: John Mark
overview: Companion of Paul and Barnabas who left their mission at Perga and returned to Jerusalem. His departure led to their disagreement over taking him again. Paul later asked for Mark, saying he was useful in ministry.

card.role: Missionary companion of Paul and Barnabas

details.label: Family
details.value: Son of Mary, whose house hosted believers in prayer; cousin of Barnabas

card.note: Traditionally identified as the author of the Gospel of Mark. The Bible doesn't name that Gospel's author.

events.title: Assists Paul and Barnabas as they proclaim God's word in Cyprus
Leaves the team at Perga and returns to Jerusalem
Sails with Barnabas to Cyprus after Paul objects to taking him again
Sends greetings with Paul, who tells the church to welcome him
Paul asks Timothy to bring Mark because he is useful in ministry

label: Jotham
overview: Uzziah's son and king of Judah for sixteen years. He governed during his father's leprosy, did what was right before the LORD, rebuilt the temple's Upper Gate and defeated the Ammonites.

details.label: Role
details.value: King of Judah; reigned in Jerusalem sixteen years

details.label: Family
details.value: Son of Uzziah and Jerushah; father of Ahaz

events.title: Governs Judah while Uzziah lives in isolation with leprosy
Succeeds Uzziah as king and does what is right before the LORD
Rebuilds the temple's Upper Gate and builds cities, fortresses and towers
Defeats the Ammonites, who pay tribute for three years
The LORD begins sending Rezin and Pekah against Judah during his reign
Dies after a sixteen-year reign, and his son Ahaz succeeds him

label: Kohath
overview: Kohath was the second son of Levi and the founder of the Kohathite clan, which held the most sacred responsibilities among the Levites. His lineage was particularly distinguished, as he was the grandfather of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. In the wilderness, the Kohathites were uniquely tasked with transporting the most holy objects of the Tabernacle, including the Ark of the Covenant and the golden lampstand. Because of the extreme holiness of these items, the Kohathites were forbidden from touching or even looking at them directly, carrying them on their shoulders using poles. Kohath’s legacy is central to the organization of Israel's worship and the preservation of the priestly line.

events.title: Migration to Egypt
events.summary: Kohath is listed among the family of Jacob who traveled to Egypt to escape the famine.
developments: He is identified as one of the three sons of Levi (Genesis 46:11)
He enters Egypt with his brothers Gershon and Merari (Genesis 46:11)
His birth preceded the long period of Israelite bondage (Genesis 46:11)
He represents the foundational generation of the Levite tribe in Egypt (Genesis 46:8-11)
events.significance: Kohath was a primary link between the era of the patriarchs and the era of the Exodus.

events.title: Establishing the Lineage
events.summary: The genealogy of Kohath is recorded, identifying him as the ancestor of Israel's greatest leaders.
developments: He lived for a total of 133 years (Exodus 6:18)
He fathered four sons: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel (Exodus 6:18)
His son Amram became the father of Moses and Aaron (Exodus 6:20)
This established the Kohathites as the family of the High Priest (Exodus 6:16-20)
events.significance: Kohath’s line became the source of both the prophetic and priestly authority in Israel.

events.title: The Sacred Commission
events.summary: God assigns the Kohathite clan the responsibility of caring for the most holy things.
developments: The Kohathites encamp on the south side of the Tabernacle (Numbers 3:29)
They are responsible for the Ark, the table, the lampstand, and the altars (Numbers 3:31)
They must carry these items on their shoulders rather than on wagons (Numbers 7:9)
They are warned that touching the holy things will result in death (Numbers 4:15)
events.significance: Their role emphasized the terrifying holiness of the divine presence.

events.title: The Rebellion of Korah
events.summary: A prominent descendant of Kohath leads a revolt against the authority of Moses and Aaron.
developments: Korah was the son of Izhar, the son of Kohath (Numbers 16:1)
He challenges the exclusive priesthood of Aaron’s family (Numbers 16:3)
The rebellion results in divine judgment by fire and the opening of the earth (Numbers 16:31-35)
This tragedy served as a warning to all Kohathites regarding their boundaries (Numbers 16:40)
events.significance: The event highlighted the internal tribal tensions within the house of Kohath.

events.title: Allotment of Cities
events.summary: The Kohathites receive a prestigious distribution of cities within the Promised Land.
developments: The first lot for the Levites falls to the families of the Kohathites (Joshua 21:4)
The priestly branch (descendants of Aaron) receives thirteen cities (Joshua 21:4)
The remaining Kohathites receive ten cities in Ephraim, Dan, and Manasseh (Joshua 21:5)
Their cities include the strategic and ancient site of Shechem (Joshua 21:20-21)
events.significance: The Kohathites were strategically placed in the heart of the nation's territory.

events.title: Musical and Liturgical Legacy
events.summary: The Kohathites continue to lead the nation's worship through music during the monarchy.
developments: Heman the singer is identified as a descendant of Kohath (1 Chronicles 6:33)
They are among the musicians appointed by David for the house of the Lord (1 Chronicles 6:31-32)
They are involved in the spiritual reforms of King Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 29:12-14)
Their lineage remains central to the Temple's operational staff (1 Chronicles 9:31-32)
events.significance: The family transitioned from wilderness carriers to permanent Temple ministers.

label: Levite
overview: A Levite was a member of the tribe of Levi, the third son of Jacob and Leah, specially set apart by God for religious service. Unlike the other tribes, the Levites were not given a specific territorial inheritance in the Promised Land; instead, they were scattered among forty-eight cities to serve as teachers of the Law and guardians of the sanctuary. Within the tribe, a specific distinction existed: while all priests had to be Levites (descended from Aaron), not all Levites were priests. Those who were not of Aaron's immediate line served as assistants, musicians, gatekeepers, and administrators. The Levites represent the concept of a people 'wholly given' to the Lord to facilitate the worship and holiness of the entire nation.

events.title: The Zeal of Levi
events.summary: The tribe of Levi distinguishes itself by choosing the Lord's side during the golden calf rebellion.
developments: Moses calls for those on the Lord's side to gather to him (Exodus 32:26)
All the sons of Levi assemble together to support Moses (Exodus 32:26)
They execute 3,000 idolaters at Moses' command (Exodus 32:27-28)
Moses declares they have ordained themselves for God's service (Exodus 32:29)
events.significance: This act of loyalty transformed the tribe's legacy from one of violence to one of consecrated service.

events.title: Substitution for the Firstborn
events.summary: God formally claims the Levites as His own, taking them in place of the firstborn sons of Israel.
developments: The Lord commands Moses to number the Levites (Numbers 3:15)
God says, 'I have taken the Levites... instead of every firstborn' (Numbers 3:12)
The total number of Levites is recorded as 22,000 (Numbers 3:39)
They are presented to Aaron to do the service of the Tabernacle (Numbers 3:6-9)
events.significance: The Levites became a living sacrifice representing the entire nation's debt to God.

events.title: Wilderness Logistics
events.summary: The Levites are organized into three main clans to manage the transport of the Tabernacle.
developments: The Kohathites carry the most holy furniture on their shoulders (Numbers 4:4-15)
The Gershonites transport the curtains and coverings (Numbers 4:24-26)
The Merarites handle the frames, pillars, and bases (Numbers 4:31-32)
Ithamar the priest oversees the Gershonites and Merarites (Numbers 4:28, 33)
events.significance: Their orderly work ensured the safe movement of God's presence through the desert.

events.title: The Ritual of Cleansing
events.summary: The Levites undergo a unique ceremony of purification before beginning their official duties.
developments: They are sprinkled with water of purification and shave their bodies (Numbers 8:7)
They wash their clothes and offer two bulls as sacrifices (Numbers 8:8, 12)
The people of Israel lay their hands on the Levites (Numbers 8:10)
Aaron offers them as a 'wave offering' before the Lord (Numbers 8:11)
events.significance: The ceremony emphasized that those who touch holy things must be set apart from the common.

events.title: Inheritance of the Lord
events.summary: God defines the Levites' portion, establishing that they will have no landed territory.
developments: The Lord tells Aaron that the Levites shall have no inheritance in the land (Numbers 18:20)
God declares: 'I am your portion and your inheritance' (Numbers 18:20)
The Levites receive the tithes of the people as their wages for service (Numbers 18:21-24)
They are required to give a tithe of the tithe to the priests (Numbers 18:26-28)
events.significance: Their lack of land made them uniquely dependent on God and the community's faithfulness.

events.title: The Levitical Cities
events.summary: The Levites are assigned forty-eight cities scattered throughout the territories of the other tribes.
developments: The heads of the Levite houses approach Joshua at Shiloh (Joshua 21:1-2)
Israel gives the Levites cities and pasturelands out of their own inheritance (Joshua 21:3)
The distribution includes the six Cities of Refuge (Joshua 21:13, 21, 27, 32, 36, 38)
This fulfilled the prophecy that they would be 'scattered in Israel' (Genesis 49:7)
events.significance: Their scattering ensured that spiritual leadership was accessible to every Israelite.

events.title: Davidic Reorganization
events.summary: King David reorganizes the Levites into specialized divisions for the coming Temple service.
developments: David numbers the Levites thirty years old and upward (1 Chronicles 23:3)
He assigns 24,000 to oversee the work of the Temple (1 Chronicles 23:4)
He appoints 4,000 as gatekeepers and 4,000 as musicians (1 Chronicles 23:5)
He designates 6,000 as officers and judges (1 Chronicles 23:4)
events.significance: This transition transformed the Levites from wilderness laborers into professional ministers of art and law.

events.title: Champions of Reform
events.summary: The Levites play a central role in the spiritual revivals of the later Judean kings.
developments: They assist Hezekiah in cleansing the Temple and restoring worship (2 Chronicles 29:12-15)
The Levites are noted as being 'more upright in heart' to consecrate themselves than the priests (2 Chronicles 29:34)
They lead the singing during the Great Passover (2 Chronicles 30:21-22)
They manage the collection and distribution of tithes and offerings (2 Chronicles 31:11-19)
events.significance: The Levites often served as the moral conscience of the nation during periods of decline.

events.title: The Covenant of Levi
events.summary: God addresses the failures of the Levites while promising a future purification of the tribe.
developments: God reminds them of His covenant of 'peace and life' with Levi (Malachi 2:5)
He rebukes the current ministers for causing many to stumble by their instruction (Malachi 2:8)
The Lord promises to send a messenger to 'purify the sons of Levi' (Malachi 3:3)
The goal is that they may bring offerings in righteousness once again (Malachi 3:3)
events.significance: The prophecy kept alive the hope of a restored and holy ministry.

events.title: Barnabas the Levite
events.summary: A prominent Levite in the early church demonstrates the continuing spirit of sacrificial service.
developments: Joseph, a Levite of Cyprus, is introduced (Acts 4:36)
The apostles rename him Barnabas, 'Son of Encouragement' (Acts 4:36)
He sells a field he owned and brings the money to the apostles (Acts 4:37)
His act mirrored the ancient Levitical principle of having no earthly inheritance (Acts 4:36-37)
events.significance: Barnabas linked the Old Testament vocation of Levi with the new mission of the Church.

label: Levites
overview: The Levites were the descendants of Levi who were designated by God to assist the priests and manage the Tabernacle and Temple. Chosen in place of the firstborn sons of Israel, they were responsible for the physical labor of the sanctuary, including its assembly, disassembly, and transport. Beyond manual labor, the Levites served as the nation’s musicians, gatekeepers, and primary teachers of the Law. Because they were given no land of their own, they relied on the tithes of the other tribes, living in specifically designated cities throughout Israel. The history of the Levites reflects the ongoing need for dedicated spiritual infrastructure to maintain a nation's covenant relationship with God.

events.title: Consecration at Sinai
events.summary: The Levites prove their exclusive devotion to God by opposing the golden calf idolatry.
developments: Moses asks who is on the Lord's side and the Levites respond (Exodus 32:26)
They carry out a difficult judgment against their own brothers (Exodus 32:27-28)
God sets them apart for His service because of this zeal (Exodus 32:29)
This established them as the guardians of the nation's holiness (Exodus 32:26-29)
events.significance: This was the foundational moment that defined the tribe's secondary priestly role.

events.title: Organization of the Clans
events.summary: God organizes the three families of Levites to handle the various components of the Tabernacle.
developments: The Kohathites are given charge of the furniture and holy objects (Numbers 3:31)
The Gershonites manage the curtains and soft structures (Numbers 3:25-26)
The Merarites handle the heavy frames, bars, and pillars (Numbers 3:36-37)
Each group is assigned a specific camping position around the sanctuary (Numbers 3:23-38)
events.significance: Their structure allowed the presence of God to be portable and orderly.

events.title: The Tithe and the Portion
events.summary: The economic survival of the Levites is established through a national tithing system.
developments: God gives the Levites the tithes of the people as their inheritance (Numbers 18:21)
They are forbidden from owning land like the other tribes (Numbers 18:20)
The Lord declares He is their 'portion' among the people (Numbers 18:20)
Levites must also give a 'tithe of the tithe' to the Aaronic priests (Numbers 18:26)
events.significance: This system ensured that the tribe could focus entirely on spiritual duties.

events.title: Settlement in the Cities
events.summary: The Levites are distributed among forty-eight cities across all tribal territories.
developments: They receive cities out of each tribe's allotment by lot (Joshua 21:1-3)
Thirteen cities are given to the priests (sons of Aaron) (Joshua 21:4)
Thirty-five cities are given to the remaining Levite families (Joshua 21:5-7)
This fulfilled the prophecy of being scattered through the nation (Genesis 49:7)
events.significance: Their geographic spread made the Law and local justice available to every citizen.

events.title: The Guild of Musicians
events.summary: King David commissions the Levites to lead the nation in musical worship.
developments: David selects 288 skilled musicians to lead in song (1 Chronicles 25:1, 7)
The clans of Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman are appointed as leads (1 Chronicles 25:1)
They use cymbals, lyres, and harps to 'prophesy' with music (1 Chronicles 25:1-3)
The musicians are organized into twenty-four divisions for rotation (1 Chronicles 25:9-31)
events.significance: This established the permanent liturgical and artistic heritage of Israel.

events.title: Migration to Judah
events.summary: When the kingdom divides, the Levites flee the northern idolatry to stay with the house of David.
developments: Jeroboam I rejects the Levites and creates his own priesthood (2 Chronicles 11:14)
Levites from all over the north leave their pasturelands for Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 11:14)
They strengthen the Kingdom of Judah for three years (2 Chronicles 11:17)
Their presence helped preserve the true worship of Yahweh in the south (2 Chronicles 11:13-17)
events.significance: The Levites' exodus from the north signaled the spiritual death of the ten tribes.

events.title: Teachers of the Word
events.summary: After the exile, the Levites play a crucial role in explaining the Scriptures to the people.
developments: Ezra reads the Law from a wooden platform (Nehemiah 8:4)
The Levites circulate through the crowd to explain the meaning (Nehemiah 8:7)
They help the people understand the words so they can respond (Nehemiah 8:8)
They encourage the people to rejoice because the joy of the Lord is their strength (Nehemiah 8:9-12)
events.significance: The Levites acted as the indispensable bridge between the written Word and the common people.

events.title: The Parable of the Good Samaritan
events.summary: Jesus uses the image of a Levite to critique religious indifference.
developments: A man is left half dead on the road to Jericho (Luke 10:30)
A priest passes by on the other side (Luke 10:31)
A Levite comes to the place, looks at him, and also passes by (Luke 10:32)
Jesus contrasts their behavior with the compassion of a Samaritan (Luke 10:33-37)
events.significance: This served as a warning that ritual status is meaningless without active love.

label: Lot
overview: Abraham's nephew, called righteous and rescued from Sodom before God destroyed it. He offered his daughters to the mob threatening his guests. Later, his daughters got him drunk and bore his sons Moab and Ben-ammi.

details.label: Family
details.value: Father of Moab and Ben-ammi by his two daughters

events.title: Chooses the Jordan plain and settles near Sodom
Is captured in war and rescued by Abram
Offers his daughters to the mob threatening his guests
Escapes to Zoar before Sodom's destruction, but his wife looks back
Fathers sons by his daughters while too drunk to know what happens

label: Luke
overview: A physician and Paul's fellow worker. He sent greetings in Paul's letters and was with Paul when Paul wrote that his departure was near.

details.label: Role
details.value: Physician and fellow worker of Paul

card.note: Traditionally identified as the writer of Luke and Acts. Their openings do not name their writer (Luke 1:1-4; Acts 1:1).

label: Lydia
overview: Sold purple cloth and came from Thyatira. In Philippi, the Lord opened her heart to Paul's message, and she and her household were baptized. She welcomed the missionaries into her home, where Paul and Silas later met other believers.

details.label: Role
details.value: Dealer in purple cloth; worshiper of God

events.title: Responds to Paul's message, is baptized with her household and welcomes the missionaries
Paul and Silas visit her house after leaving prison to encourage the believers

label: Lysias
overview: Commanded the Roman regiment in Jerusalem and rescued Paul from a mob. He ordered Paul flogged but was alarmed to learn he had chained a Roman citizen, then sent him under guard to Felix after a murder plot was reported.

details.label: Role
details.value: Commander of the Roman regiment in Jerusalem

events.title: Rescues and arrests Paul, initially mistaking him for an Egyptian rebel
Orders Paul flogged, then learns that he is a Roman citizen
Brings Paul before the Sanhedrin and removes him when the dispute turns violent
Sends Paul under guard to Felix after learning of a murder plot

label: Macedonians
overview: The Macedonians were the inhabitants of the Roman province of Macedonia, located in modern-day northern Greece and the Balkans. They played a vital role in the early church as the first Europeans to receive the Gospel after Paul’s 'Macedonian Vision.' Known for their generosity despite 'extreme poverty,' the Macedonian churches in Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea became models of sacrificial giving and steadfastness under persecution. They provided consistent financial and emotional support for Paul's mission and were the primary contributors to the collection for the suffering believers in Jerusalem. The Macedonians represent the successful transition of Christianity into a Western and international context.

events.title: The Macedonian Call
events.summary: A supernatural vision directs Paul to bring the Gospel to the region of Macedonia.
developments: A vision appears to Paul in the night at Troas (Acts 16:9)
A 'man of Macedonia' is seen standing and pleading (Acts 16:9)
The man says, 'Come over to Macedonia and help us' (Acts 16:9)
Paul and his team immediately depart, concluding God had called them (Acts 16:10)
events.significance: This vision shifted the center of gravity for the early church toward Europe.

events.title: The Church in Philippi
events.summary: The Gospel takes root in a major Macedonian city through the conversion of Lydia and a jailer.
developments: Philippi is identified as a leading city of the district (Acts 16:12)
Lydia and her household are the first converts (Acts 16:14-15)
Paul and Silas are imprisoned after casting out a spirit of divination (Acts 16:16-24)
The jailer and his family believe after a miraculous earthquake (Acts 16:25-34)
events.significance: Philippi became the most loyal and supportive church in the Macedonian region.

events.title: The Thessalonian Uproar
events.summary: The Gospel spreads to the capital of Macedonia, triggering significant political and social conflict.
developments: Paul preaches in the synagogue for three Sabbaths (Acts 17:1-3)
A great many Greeks and leading women join the faith (Acts 17:4)
Opposition Jews incite a mob, claiming the believers serve another king, Jesus (Acts 17:5-7)
The converts are praised for receiving the word in much affliction (1 Thessalonians 1:6)
events.significance: The Thessalonian Macedonians became a model for endurance under social pressure.

events.title: The Noble Bereans
events.summary: Macedonians in Berea are singled out for their intellectual and spiritual integrity.
developments: The Bereans are described as 'more noble' than those in Thessalonica (Acts 17:11)
They receive the word with all eagerness (Acts 17:11)
They examine the Scriptures daily to see if Paul's teaching is true (Acts 17:11)
Many of them believe, including prominent Greek women and men (Acts 17:12)
events.significance: The Berean Macedonians established the biblical standard for critical engagement with teaching.

events.title: The Grace of Giving
events.summary: Paul uses the Macedonian churches as the definitive example of sacrificial financial support.
developments: The churches are described as being in a 'severe test of affliction' (2 Corinthians 8:2)
Their 'extreme poverty' overflowed in a wealth of generosity (2 Corinthians 8:2)
They gave 'beyond their means' and begged for the favor of taking part (2 Corinthians 8:3-4)
They gave 'themselves first to the Lord' (2 Corinthians 8:5)
events.significance: The Macedonians provided the theological blueprint for New Testament stewardship.

events.title: The Collection for Jerusalem
events.summary: Macedonian believers lead the international effort to provide relief for the Judean church.
developments: Macedonia and Achaia make a contribution for the poor in Jerusalem (Romans 15:26)
Sopater of Berea and Aristarchus of Thessalonica join Paul's delegation (Acts 20:4)
Aristarchus remains with Paul as a fellow prisoner in Rome (Colossians 4:10)
The gift fulfilled a debt of gratitude for spiritual blessings received from Israel (Romans 15:27)
events.significance: Their generosity helped unify the Jewish and Gentile branches of the global church.

label: Magi
overview: The Magi were a group of distinguished and learned men from the East who traveled to Jerusalem following a celestial phenomenon to worship the 'King of the Jews.' Often described as 'wise men,' they were likely astronomers or priestly scholars from Persia or Babylon. Their arrival triggered a crisis in the court of Herod the Great, as they sought the promised Messiah based on ancient prophecies and the sighting of a unique star. Upon finding the child Jesus in Bethlehem, they presented him with symbolic gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh. The Magi represent the first Gentile recognition of Jesus' kingship and the international scope of His mission.

events.title: The Arrival in Jerusalem
events.summary: A group of Magi arrive at the Judean capital inquiring about a newborn king.
developments: They come from 'the East' (Matthew 2:1)
They ask: 'Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?' (Matthew 2:2)
They explain they saw 'his star' when it rose (Matthew 2:2)
Their presence causes King Herod and all Jerusalem to be 'troubled' (Matthew 2:3)
events.significance: Their inquiry signaled that the Messiah's birth was an event of global importance.

events.title: The Secret Audience
events.summary: King Herod summons the Magi to discover the exact timing of the child's birth.
developments: Herod asks the chief priests where the Christ was to be born (Matthew 2:4)
The priests identify Bethlehem based on the prophet Micah (Matthew 2:5-6)
Herod meets the Magi secretly to ascertain the time the star appeared (Matthew 2:7)
He deceptively tells them to report back so he can 'worship' the child (Matthew 2:8)
events.significance: The Magi were caught in the middle of a political and spiritual power struggle.

events.title: The Journey to Bethlehem
events.summary: The star reappears, leading the Magi to the specific location of the infant Jesus.
developments: They follow the star as it goes before them (Matthew 2:9)
The star stops over the place where the child was (Matthew 2:9)
The Magi rejoice with 'exceedingly great joy' (Matthew 2:10)
They find the child with Mary his mother in a house (Matthew 2:11)
events.significance: This was the first physical encounter between Gentile seekers and the Messiah.

events.title: Worship and Gifts
events.summary: The Magi perform a ritual act of homage and present expensive, symbolic treasures.
developments: They fall down and worship the child (Matthew 2:11)
They open their treasures and offer gifts of gold (Matthew 2:11)
They present frankincense (Matthew 2:11)
They present myrrh (Matthew 2:11)
events.significance: The gifts recognized Jesus' roles as King (gold), Priest (incense), and Suffering Savior (myrrh).

events.title: Divine Warning and Departure
events.summary: Being warned in a dream, the Magi outmaneuver Herod and return home safely.
developments: They are warned in a dream not to return to Herod (Matthew 2:12)
They depart for their own country by another way (Matthew 2:12)
Their departure leaves Herod furious and triggers the massacre of the innocents (Matthew 2:16)
This was the final biblical mention of the eastern scholars (Matthew 2:12)
events.significance: Their obedience protected the infant Jesus from an early assassination attempt.

label: Magog
overview: Magog is a name used in the Bible for both a descendant of Noah and a geographical or symbolic territory associated with the final enemies of God. First appearing in the Table of Nations, Magog was a son of Japheth and the father of the peoples inhabiting the regions north of Israel. In the prophecies of Ezekiel, Magog is the land from which the prince Gog launches his massive end-times invasion. This imagery is carried into the New Testament Book of Revelation, where 'Gog and Magog' represent the collective nations of the world that gather for a final, futile rebellion against the Kingdom of Christ.

events.title: Ancestral Origin
events.summary: Magog is established as one of the foundational ancestors of the human race after the Flood.
developments: He is identified as the second son of Japheth (Genesis 10:2)
Japheth was the son of Noah (Genesis 10:1)
Magog is grouped with Gomer, Madai, and Javan (Genesis 10:2)
His descendants settle in the northern and western lands (Genesis 10:2-5)
events.significance: Magog represents the ethnic root of the northern 'Gentile' nations.

events.title: The Land of the Invader
events.summary: Prophetic literature identifies Magog as the base of operations for a future world enemy.
developments: The word of the Lord comes against 'Gog, of the land of Magog' (Ezekiel 38:2)
Magog is described as a region in the 'uttermost parts of the north' (Ezekiel 38:6, 15)
The inhabitants are depicted as a vast, well-armed horse-riding host (Ezekiel 38:15)
The invasion is directed against a restored and peaceful Israel (Ezekiel 38:8-12)
events.significance: Magog became the geographic symbol for the origin of anti-theocratic aggression.

events.title: Judgment on the Territory
events.summary: God promises to send fire upon the homeland of the invaders as part of His cosmic judgment.
developments: God says He will send fire on Magog (Ezekiel 39:6)
The judgment reaches those who 'dwell securely in the coastlands' (Ezekiel 39:6)
The goal is that the nations 'shall know that I am the Lord' (Ezekiel 39:6)
The destruction is complete and supernatural (Ezekiel 39:1-8)
events.significance: The fall of Magog demonstrated that God’s justice reaches even the most distant lands.

events.title: Symbol of Global Rebellion
events.summary: In the final prophecy of the Bible, the name is used to describe the totality of unrepentant nations.
developments: After the thousand years, Satan is released from prison (Revelation 20:7)
He goes out to deceive the nations in the four corners of the earth (Revelation 20:8)
The nations are collectively called 'Gog and Magog' (Revelation 20:8)
Their number is described as being like the sand of the sea (Revelation 20:8)
events.significance: The term transitioned from a specific ethnicity to a universal symbol of human opposition to God.

events.title: The Final Consummation
events.summary: The forces of Magog are consumed by fire in the ultimate conclusion of human history.
developments: They surround the camp of the saints and the beloved city (Revelation 20:9)
Fire comes down from heaven and consumes them (Revelation 20:9)
The devil who deceived them is thrown into the lake of fire (Revelation 20:10)
This event leads directly to the Great White Throne judgment (Revelation 20:11)
events.significance: The story of Magog ends with the total and eternal victory of God's Kingdom.

label: Maher-shalal-hash-baz
overview: Born to Isaiah and the prophetess, and given his name by the LORD's command. God said that before the boy could call for his father or mother, Assyria's king would carry off the wealth of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria.

card.role: Isaiah's son named by God's command

details.label: Family
details.value: Son of Isaiah and the prophetess

label: Mahlon
overview: Moved from Bethlehem to Moab with his parents during a famine and married Ruth. He died there, leaving Ruth widowed. Boaz later acquired the family property and married Ruth to preserve Mahlon's name with his inheritance.

details.label: Family
details.value: Son of Elimelech and Naomi, brother of Chilion

label: Malchus
overview: Served the high priest and was present at Jesus' arrest. Peter cut off his right ear with a sword. Jesus stopped the violence, touched the ear and healed him.

card.role: High priest's servant healed by Jesus

label: Manasseh
overview: Manasseh was the firstborn son of Joseph and the founder of one of the largest tribes of Israel. Though the elder brother, he received a secondary blessing from his grandfather Jacob, who prophetically placed him behind his younger brother, Ephraim. The tribe of Manasseh was uniquely divided, with half settling in the fertile Transjordan and half within Canaan. Centuries later, another Manasseh reigned as the fourteenth king of Judah. His fifty-five-year reign was the longest and most wicked in Judah's history, characterized by extreme idolatry and the shedding of innocent blood. Despite his profound evil, the biblical record ends his story with a remarkable account of his repentance and restoration after being taken captive by the Assyrians.

events.title: Birth in Egypt
events.summary: Manasseh is born to Joseph and Asenath during the seven years of abundance.
developments: He is the firstborn son of Joseph (Genesis 41:51)
Joseph names him Manasseh, meaning 'Making to Forget' (Genesis 41:51)
Joseph says, 'God has made me forget all my hardship' (Genesis 41:51)
He is raised in the highest level of Egyptian nobility (Genesis 41:45-51)
events.significance: Manasseh represented the first generation of Joseph's line born into success rather than slavery.

events.title: The Crossed-Hand Blessing
events.summary: Jacob bypasses Manasseh's birthright to give the primary blessing to his younger brother.
developments: Joseph places Manasseh at Jacob's right hand (Genesis 48:13)
Jacob crosses his hands, putting his left on Manasseh (Genesis 48:14)
Joseph attempts to correct his father (Genesis 48:17-18)
Jacob insists, prophesying that while Manasseh shall be great, his brother shall be greater (Genesis 48:19)
events.significance: This established the historical precedence of Ephraim over Manasseh in the tribal hierarchy.

events.title: The Divided Inheritance
events.summary: The tribe of Manasseh settles on both sides of the Jordan River.
developments: The descendants of Machir (Manasseh) conquer Gilead (Numbers 32:39-40)
Half the tribe receives an enormous territory in Bashan and Gilead (Joshua 13:29-31)
The other half receives a lot in central Canaan near Ephraim (Joshua 17:1-11)
They complain to Joshua that their allotment is too small for their numbers (Joshua 17:14-15)
events.significance: Manasseh was the only tribe to hold significant territory both inside and outside the Promised Land proper.

events.title: The Wicked King
events.summary: King Manasseh succeeds Hezekiah and systematically undoes his father’s reforms.
developments: He becomes king at age twelve and reigns fifty-five years (2 Kings 21:1)
He rebuilds the high places and builds altars for Baal (2 Kings 21:3)
He practices fortune-telling and consults mediums (2 Kings 21:6)
He burns his own son as an offering to idols (2 Kings 21:6)
events.significance: Manasseh's reign was the spiritual 'point of no return' that guaranteed the Babylonian exile.

events.title: Shedding Innocent Blood
events.summary: Manasseh fills Jerusalem with violence, reportedly executing the faithful including prophets.
developments: He is noted for shedding 'very much innocent blood' (2 Kings 21:16)
He filled the city from one end to the other with blood (2 Kings 21:16)
The prophets warned that God would 'wipe Jerusalem as one wipes a dish' (2 Kings 21:10-13)
His crimes were cited as the primary reason God would not forgive Judah (2 Kings 24:3-4)
events.significance: He represents the peak of institutionalized evil within the house of David.

events.title: Captivity and Repentance
events.summary: Taken prisoner by the Assyrians, Manasseh humbles himself and experiences a miracle of grace.
developments: Assyrian commanders take him to Babylon with hooks and chains (2 Chronicles 33:11)
In his distress, he entreated the favor of the Lord (2 Chronicles 33:12)
God was moved by his entreaty and restored him to his kingdom (2 Chronicles 33:13)
Manasseh then knew that 'the Lord is God' (2 Chronicles 33:13)
events.significance: His restoration is the most dramatic example of individual repentance and divine forgiveness in the Old Testament.

events.title: The King’s Reforms
events.summary: Following his return, Manasseh attempts to purge the idols he had previously championed.
developments: He builds an outer wall for the City of David (2 Chronicles 33:14)
He removes the foreign gods and the idol from the Temple (2 Chronicles 33:15)
He repairs the altar of the Lord and offers sacrifices (2 Chronicles 33:16)
He commands Judah to serve the Lord God of Israel (2 Chronicles 33:16)
events.significance: Manasseh ended his life as a reformer, though he could not erase his previous impact.

label: Manoah
overview: Lived in Zorah and became Samson's father. After an angel promised his wife a son, he asked God for guidance in raising the child. He saw the angel ascend in an offering's flame and later objected to Samson's choice of a Philistine wife.

details.label: Family
details.value: From the Danite clan; father of Samson

details.label: Buried
details.value: His tomb was between Zorah and Eshtaol

events.title: Prays for guidance and meets the messenger who spoke to his wife
Sees the angel ascend in the flame and fears that he will die
His wife gives birth to Samson
Objects with his wife to Samson's proposed Philistine marriage

label: Many
overview: The term 'many' is used throughout the Bible to signify a vast, often unnumbered multitude that is impacted by the actions or words of a few. In the Old Testament, it frequently describes the nations that would be blessed through Abraham or the crowds that witnessed the mighty works of the prophets. In the New Testament, 'the many' carries a deep theological weight, particularly regarding the atonement. Jesus stated that He came to give His life as a 'ransom for many,' and Paul contrasted the 'many' who died through Adam with the 'many' who receive grace and life through Christ. This concept emphasizes the expansive and inclusive reach of God’s redemptive plan.

events.title: Father of Many Nations
events.summary: God changes Abram's name to signify his role as the ancestor of a vast multitude.
developments: God makes a covenant with Abram (Genesis 17:2-4)
His name is changed to Abraham (Genesis 17:5)
The reason is given: 'for I have made you the father of a multitude (many) of nations' (Genesis 17:5)
The promise includes kings and people groups beyond Israel (Genesis 17:6)
events.significance: The 'many' are the intended recipients of the patriarchal blessing.

events.title: Justifying the Many
events.summary: The prophet Isaiah describes the Suffering Servant’s work as having a broad impact on the guilty.
developments: The Servant will 'sprinkle many nations' (Isaiah 52:15)
By his knowledge shall the righteous one 'make many to be accounted righteous' (Isaiah 53:11)
He shall bear the iniquities of 'the many' (Isaiah 53:11)
He bore the sin of 'many' and makes intercession for the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12)
events.significance: This prophecy established the 'many' as the collective body of the redeemed.

events.title: A Ransom for Many
events.summary: Jesus defines the purpose of His mission in terms of a substitutionary payment for a multitude.
developments: Jesus speaks to His disciples about true greatness and service (Matthew 20:25-27)
He declares the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve (Matthew 20:28)
He says He will give His life as a 'ransom for many' (Mark 10:45)
The term identifies the global scope of the benefits of His death (Matthew 20:28)
events.significance: Jesus explicitly linked His sacrifice to the 'many' of Isaiah's prophecy.

events.title: The Cup of the Many
events.summary: During the Last Supper, Jesus connects the wine of the New Covenant to the forgiveness of many.
developments: He takes the cup and gives thanks (Matthew 26:27)
He calls it 'my blood of the covenant' (Matthew 26:28)
He says it is 'poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins' (Matthew 26:28)
This formalized the liturgical recognition of the 'many' in the church (Matthew 26:26-28)
events.significance: The New Covenant was founded on the inclusive grace shown to the many.

events.title: The Two 'Manys'
events.summary: Paul compares the universal impact of Adam’s sin with the universal offer of Christ’s righteousness.
developments: Many died through the one man’s (Adam) trespass (Romans 5:15)
The grace of God and the gift by Christ abounded for 'the many' (Romans 5:15)
By one man’s disobedience the 'many' were made sinners (Romans 5:19)
By one man’s obedience the 'many' will be made righteous (Romans 5:19)
events.significance: Paul used the concept of 'the many' to explain the architecture of salvation history.

events.title: The Final Sacrifice
events.summary: The author of Hebrews summarizes the finality of Christ's work for the many.
developments: Christ was offered once to bear the sins of 'many' (Hebrews 9:28)
He will appear a second time to save those who wait for Him (Hebrews 9:28)
This contrasts with the repeated animal sacrifices that could not perfect the conscience (Hebrews 9:11-14)
The 'many' are the final beneficiaries of the High Priestly work of Jesus (Hebrews 9:24-28)
events.significance: The story of the 'many' concludes with their eternal security through one sacrifice.

label: Martha
overview: Mary and Lazarus's sister, from Bethany. She welcomed Jesus but complained when Mary listened while she served, and He corrected her. After Lazarus died, she confessed that Jesus was the Christ and the Son of God.

events.title: Complains about serving alone, and Jesus defends Mary's choice to listen
Meets Jesus after Lazarus's death and confesses Him as Christ and Son of God
Warns of the odor at Lazarus's tomb before Jesus raises him
Serves at a dinner for Jesus, with Lazarus at the table

label: Nabal
overview: Wealthy Calebite from Maon, harsh and evil in his dealings, who refused David's request for provisions. His wife Abigail prevented David from killing his men. After she told Nabal what happened, his heart failed, and the LORD later struck him dead.

details.label: From
details.value: Maon; had his business in Carmel

events.title: Refuses David's request for food, and David prepares to attack
Holds a drunken feast; his heart fails after Abigail tells him what happened
The LORD strikes him dead about ten days later

label: Naboth
overview: Owned a vineyard beside Ahab's palace in Jezreel and refused to give up his family inheritance. Jezebel arranged false accusations that he had cursed God and the king. He was stoned to death, and Ahab took his vineyard.

card.role: Vineyard owner murdered through Jezebel's plot

details.label: Role
details.value: Owner of a vineyard beside Ahab's palace

events.title: Refuses Ahab's offer to buy or exchange his vineyard
Is falsely accused and stoned, and Ahab takes his vineyard

label: Nadab
overview: Nadab refers to two significant figures whose lives ended in judgment: the eldest son of Aaron the priest and the second king of the northern kingdom of Israel. Nadab, son of Aaron, was struck dead by divine fire for offering 'unauthorized fire' in the Tabernacle, an event that established the severe standards of holiness for the priesthood. Centuries later, Nadab, son of Jeroboam I, reigned for only two years before being assassinated during a siege by Baasha. His death marked the violent end of the first dynasty of the northern kingdom, fulfilling the prophecy of doom against the house of Jeroboam. Both figures serve as biblical warnings about the consequences of religious and political rebellion.

events.title: Privilege at Sinai
events.summary: Nadab, son of Aaron, is chosen as one of the few to ascend the mountain and see God’s glory.
developments: God calls Moses, Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu (Exodus 24:1)
They see the God of Israel with a pavement of sapphire under His feet (Exodus 24:9-10)
They eat and drink in the presence of God (Exodus 24:11)
He is consecrated as a priest alongside his father and brothers (Exodus 28:1)
events.significance: Nadab began his ministry with a level of revelation shared by very few in history.

events.title: The Unauthorized Fire
events.summary: Nadab commits a fatal ritual error during the inauguration of the Tabernacle service.
developments: He and Abihu take their censers and put fire and incense in them (Leviticus 10:1)
They offer 'unauthorized fire' which the Lord had not commanded (Leviticus 10:1)
Fire comes out from before the Lord and consumes them (Leviticus 10:2)
They die instantly in the presence of the Lord (Leviticus 10:2)
events.significance: His death was the definitive lesson on the necessity of strict obedience in worship.

events.title: The Aftermath of Judgment

label: Ornan
overview: Ornan (also known as Araunah) was a Jebusite resident of Jerusalem who owned a strategically located threshing floor on Mount Moriah. During the plague that followed King David’s census sin, the Angel of the Lord stopped at Ornan’s property. Witnessing the divine messenger, Ornan offered to give David his land and livestock for free as a sacrifice to stop the pestilence. David refused to offer that which 'cost him nothing' and purchased the site at a fair price. This threshing floor became the site for David's atoning altar and the future location of Solomon’s Temple, making Ornan’s property the spiritual center of the world for centuries.
